#3086. OMS Energy (OMSE) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript

Saudi order delays, record cash and a services shift shape this quarter's results.

By Motley Fool Transcribing – Nov 26, 2026 at 9:53AM EST

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

OMS Energy (OMSE +6.67%) reported a decrease in revenue for the first half of fiscal year 2027 but expanded its gross margin while maintaining a debt-free balance sheet with record cash reserves. Management attributed the revenue decline primarily to procurement delays in Saudi Arabia, where orders under a long-term supply agreement are being deferred instead of canceled. The company is actively diversifying its geographic footprint with new orders in Malaysia, Kuwait, and Pakistan while shifting toward a higher-margin services revenue mix. Strategic efforts focus on cost discipline and cash generation to manage through extended customer decision cycles.

Operator: Hello, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you for joining OMS Energy Technologies, Inc.'s Earnings Presentation for the first half of fiscal year 2027. Today's presentation is being recorded. The company's financial and operating results for the 6 months ended September 30, 2026, have been released and are available on the OMS Investor Relations website at ir.omsos.com. Please note that today's discussion will contain forward-looking statements made under the safe harbor provisions of the U.S. Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. These statements typically contain words such as may, will, expect, target, estimate, intend, believe, potential, continue, or similar expressions. Forward-looking statements involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those projected or anticipated.

These include changes in customer spending and procurement, the timing of call-off orders and deliveries, geopolitical developments, supply chain conditions, and foreign exchange movements. Further information about risks is included in the company's filings with the SEC. The company does not undertake any obligation to update forward-looking information, except as required under applicable law. Today's discussion also includes adjusted EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow, which are supplemental non-IFRS measures. Their definitions and reconciliations to the most directly comparable IFRS measures are included in the earnings release. I will now turn the presentation over to Mr. Meng Hock How. Please go ahead.

Meng Hock How: Thank you, operator, and thank you to everyone joining us today. I am Meng Hock How, CEO of OMS Energy Technologies. I'll discuss our first half performance, what we're seeing in customer orders and the progress we're making across our business. I will then address several questions that we expect investors to have about the results. For investors newer to OMS, we are Singapore headquartered equipment manufacturer and engineered solutions supplier serving upstream oil and gas operators. Our core products include Surface Wellhead and Christmas Tree Systems, Specialty Connectors and Pipe. We also provide premium threading, repair, and other engineering services through 11 manufacturing facilities across 6 markets in Asia Pacific, Middle East, and North Africa. Turning to our results.

I'm pleased to report that we expanded our gross margin, generated strong cash flow and further strengthened our debt-free balance sheet in the first half. Gross margin increased to 31.4% from 28.2% in the prior year period, and net profit margin improved to 18.8% from 17.6%. We generated $25.3 million in operating cash flow and approximately twice our net profit and ended September with a record $172.3 million in cash, cash equivalents, and restricted cash or approximately $4.06 per share. We delivered these results while macro conditions remain challenging given ongoing geopolitical uncertainty and supply chain disruption in our major markets. Our facilities remained operational throughout the period.

Customers continued to tender and place orders with OMS during the half, but took longer to commit and schedule deliveries, weighing on revenue. First half revenue was $66.7 million compared with $82.8 million a year ago, largely due to the slower pace of Saudi Aramco call-off orders. This was partially offset by increased activity in Malaysia and Thailand, showing the value of our diversified footprint. In the current environment, the challenge for OMS lies not in lack of opportunities, but in reduced visibility, extended decision cycle and execution timing. You will see that pattern throughout this period's result.

With order timing harder to predict, we are concentrating on factors that we can control, including careful management of inventory, costs, and customer deliveries. By keeping inventory, purchasing and costs in line with the orders we actually received, we were able to protect profitability and generate strong cash flow despite fluctuating order volumes. Saudi Arabia is where reduced visibility and order timing have affected us most. Revenue from Specialty Connectors and Pipe was $37.1 million compared with $51.1 million a year ago as the timing of the order placed under our long-term supply agreement with Saudi Aramco continued to slow. I would like to emphasize, as previously mentioned, that these are deferred orders, not lost orders.

Our agreement with Saudi Aramco remains intact. Our relationship remains strong, and there has been no cancellation. To that end, we continue to receive business from Aramco. In September, we announced a $7.1 million order for specialty connectors and pipe won through an open tender outside our long-term agreement. Since that award, we have received a call-off order of approximately $3 million under the long-term agreement as well as a separate $500,000 order for loose connectors for Aramco's float equipment. We view these awards as a reflection of Aramco's confidence in our product and the delivery record we have built in the Kingdom over 15 years.

In Indonesia, our operation in Bogor just received an order for specialty pipe and connectors valued at approximately $396,000 for Pertamina North West Java. This is a follow-on from the order we announced in January 2026. Furthermore, our operations in Singapore and Malaysia secured their first order for specialty connectors and pipe for Petronas in Malaysia, valued at approximately $687,000. Of that amount, $367,000 was delivered during the first half of fiscal 2027. We also continue to bid for supply contracts with Kuwait Oil Company, KOC, and are actively engaged in the tender process we have entered after we qualified for the approved vendor list in July.

Also following that qualification, we received a $458,000 order from Tenaris for OMS connectors that we welded onto Tenaris pipe and supplied to Kuwait Oil Company as part of Tenaris OCTG package. While modest in size, the Petronas and Tenaris order extend our specialty connectors and pipe business to 2 more national oil companies, which we believe can lead to additional business over time. We've also recently bid to supply specialty connectors and Pipe for a development in the South China Sea with results expected next month. If we are successful, this will mark our reentry into China after more than 10 years and represent further progress in our ongoing geographic diversification efforts.

In surface wellhead and Christmas trees, we continue to win orders while revenue follows customer and project schedules. First half revenue from Surface Wellhead and Christmas Tree was $3.5 million compared to $6.2 million a year ago. Indonesia is the main market for this business and upstream activities there has been slow over the past year as new oil and gas projects have taken longer to come online. In September, we announced $2.3 million order from Pertamina Hulu Rokan under our existing 3-year supply contract following the contract extension we announced in March. We also recently received $766,000 order from Pertamina for choke valves, a component of Christmas tree systems.

Separately, we are awaiting a call-off of approximately $1 million from Pertamina under an existing contract. We also completed the stackup and function test of a new compact surface wellhead and Christmas tree system for Pertamina, a milestone in developing our wellhead product offering with an established customer. The equipment has been delivered and is being installed by Pertamina on its Tamadun-001 field, where it is carrying out an unconventional drilling program. Indonesia holds vast unconventional oil and gas resources, including shale gas, coal-bed methane, methane hydrate, and shale oil, and commercial development is still at an early stage. We believe this installation position us well as that activity develops.

OMS Singapore has also just delivered a complete 10,000 psi wellhead and Christmas tree system to Orient Petroleum in Pakistan, marking OMS Singapore's first delivery of such a system to the country. Orient Petroleum is one of Pakistan's largest private exploration and production company and has been operating since 1979. OMS Singapore has also received a supply contract for 2 sets of production tree for a Bleiswijk geothermal cluster in Netherlands. While the value is small at approximately $130,000, it is a step into the European energy sector that we want to build on. Across our service businesses, customers also continued to place orders during the half.

Other ancillary services revenue rose to $9.4 million from $7.5 million, an increase of approximately 25%, supported by repair, refurbishment, and engineering work in Thailand and Malaysia. This maintenance work depends less on new project approval than equipment sales do. Premium threading services revenue was $16.7 million compared to $18 million. Together, our services business accounted for approximately 39% of first half revenue, up from approximately 31% a year ago. In Singapore, we've also secured an approximately $0.55 million of repair work on production risers for a large oilfield services company for the upcoming Kikeh 3B Phase 2 subsea project in Malaysia. The Kikeh field is operated by PTTEP Malaysia. Our backlog reflects the period's slower order timing pattern.

At September 30, it stood at $40.9 million compared to $60.7 million at March 31, primarily due to call-off timing under the Saudi agreement. Our backlog comprises confirmed orders that have not yet been recognized as revenue and are expected to be delivered within the following 12 months. It does not include orders received after September 30, including the additional Saudi Aramco order I mentioned earlier. A framework agreement, a tender opportunity, and a confirmed call-off each represent different stages of the customer's procurement process and the backlog captures only the last of those stages. Today, opportunities are taking longer to move from tender to award and from framework agreement to call-off.

To put the backlog figure in context, Saudi Aramco maintained its 2026 capital spending guidance of $50 billion to $55 billion when it reported third quarter's results this month. Aramco attributed lower upstream spending in the quarter, mainly to the timing of crude oil increment projects and several of its major upstream developments, including the Dammam development and the second phase of Jafurah are scheduled to come on stream in 2027. Across the wider region, BMI expects oil and gas capital spending to grow about 4% this year and to average approximately 6% a year from 2027 to 2030. Now let me walk through our financial results in more detail.

First half revenue was $66.7 million compared to $82.8 million in the prior year period. Gross profit was $21 million compared to $23.3 million. Gross margin increased from 28.2% to 31.4%, supported by a more favorable mix in Saudi Specialty connectors and pipe and a greater contribution from higher-margin ancillary services in Thailand. Selling and general and administrative expenses were $7.1 million compared to $5.4 million in the prior year period. The increase primarily reflected personnel costs and professional services, governance, and compliance-related fees. Operating profit was $13.9 million compared to $17.9 million, and operating margin was 20.8% compared to 21.6%. Finance income increased to $2.4 million from $1.6 million, reflecting more cash placed in interest-earning deposits.

Income tax expense was $3.6 million compared with $4.6 million, and our effective tax rate was 22.3% compared to 24%. Net profit was $12.6 million compared with $14.6 million, and net profit margin increased to 18.8% from 17.6%. Basic and diluted earnings per share were $0.28 compared with $0.33, reflecting lower profit attributable to shareholders and a higher weighted average share count. Adjusted EBITDA was $17.3 million compared to $21.8 million. Adjusted EBITDA margin held relatively steady at 25.9% compared with 26.4% despite the 19% decline in revenue. We continue to use this supplement measure alongside the IFRS results. The earnings release sets out the adjustment and the reconciliation from net profit. Cash generation remained an area of strength.

Operating cash flow was $25.3 million compared with $26.4 million. Adjusted free cash flow was $19.9 million compared with $25.4 million. As described in our earnings release, this measure now deducts cash placed in fixed rate structured deposits, and the change from last year mainly reflects the $5 million we placed in these deposits during the period. Part of our cash generation came from a reduction in inventory, which contributed $9.5 million to operating cash flow compared to $12.2 million a year ago. Inventory ended September at $7.7 million compared to $17.2 million at March 31. The level of inventory and the timing of replenishment will affect cash flow as order activity changes.

We will continue to manage purchasing and production against the equipment needed for customer deliveries. Net cash used in investing activities was $5.4 million. This included $5 million placed in fixed rate structured deposits and approximately $0.4 million for property, plant, and equipment and software. These deposits are not included in our reported cash balance of $172.3 million. Cash and cash equivalents and restricted cash increased to a record $172.3 million at September 30 compared with $104.3 million at March 31. Our balance sheet remains free of bank borrowings. We continue to refine our capital allocation plan and assess investment opportunities while maintaining the financial flexibility to meet delivery commitments.

Looking ahead, our immediate planning reflects the slow pace of Saudi call-off and the orders we have in hand across the business. The September Aramco tender win and the Pertamina order were announced with expected delivery dates in January and March 2027, respectively. We are focused on execution against the schedule and continued engagement with our customers. We remain cautious about the timing of a wider recovery in procurement. At the same time, we are encouraged by our recent order activity, the growing contribution from our services business and the opportunities we are pursuing across the Middle East and Asia.

We have long-term agreement with leading national oil companies, 11 manufacturing facilities close to our customers and more than $172 million in cash with no debt. We believe this strength positions OMS well to capture future opportunities. Before we close, I would like to address questions investors are likely to have in the half, including how current visibility compares with the expectation that we discussed in June. Question one, how much of the earnings decline is attributable to geopolitical tensions and have projects been canceled? We have not observed material projects cancellation directly attributable to geopolitical development. The effect has been indirect primarily through longer customer decision cycle, deferred projects award and increased caution in customer capital spending decisions.

For OMS, the main operating issue has been the slower pace of Saudi call-off orders. Some customers have taken longer to finalize investment decisions or have adjusted project time lines, and it is difficult to isolate a specific financial impact. Opportunities remain in place, but decision and awards are taking longer. We are actively pursuing work in Malaysia, Indonesia, the UAE, Kuwait and China. Question two, is demand weakening, particularly in the Middle East? We would characterize the environment as one of increased caution rather than broad-based demand weakness. Activity levels vary by customers and markets. Customers continue to evaluate opportunities and pursue strategic projects, although decision-making and approval processes have become more measured.

In certain cases, this has translated into longer approval and procurement cycles. For OMS, that shows up as a slower Saudi call-off and a longer gap between tender and award. Several of the largest oilfield services have also pointed to the limited near-term visibility in the Middle East in their recent results. Even so, Saudi Aramco has maintained its 2026 capital spending guidance and has continued to award us business, including the $7.1 million tender award in September and additional orders since then. Our focus remains on supporting customers while adapting to changing market conditions. Third question, have supply chain disruption become a major concern? Supply chain conditions remain manageable, but less predictable than in previous period.

We have experienced longer lead time and occasional logistic challenges affecting certain projects. Management continues to work closely with suppliers and customers to mitigate these impacts where possible. The fourth question, how are margins holding up? And can they be sustained? Well, first half gross margin increased to 31.4% from 28.2%, supported by the mix of equipment specification and services. Operating margin was 20.8%. We continue to manage procurement, project execution and operating costs carefully. Our priority is maintaining financial discipline while remaining competitive in the markets we serve. However, if activity slows further in the second half, margins could be affected. We will continue to manage costs carefully as conditions evolve.

Question five, do we expect conditions to improve in the second half? Given the uncertain geopolitical and macroeconomic environment, we do not believe it will be appropriate to speculate on the timing or extent of any improvement. Customers continue to tender and place orders with OMS. Improvement depends on visibility returning and decision cycles shortening, and we do not control that timing. Continued uncertainty could further influence customer spending, project timing and supply chain performance. We continue to maintain long-standing customer relationships, technical capabilities and a diversified market presence. Management remains focused on factors within our control, including customer engagement, operational execution, cost management, and cash generation.

Sixth question is, does the expectation of modest FY 2027 revenue growth discussed in June still hold? Well, in June, we expected fiscal 2027 revenue to be modestly above fiscal 2026, assuming no further material geopolitical disruption. Since then, the Saudi call-off activity has remained slow and the timing of a broader pickup remains uncertain. Given the first half revenue of $66.7 million and the continued slow pace of call-off, we no longer expect fiscal 2027 revenue to exceed fiscal 2026. We're not providing a specific range today, and we will update investors as visibility on order timing improves. The last point or question 7, how do you plan to use your cash?

Well, our priorities are consistent with what we shared in June. First, we are reinvesting in core businesses, including capacity, certification, and in-region capabilities that support our growth. Second, we continue to review bolt-on acquisition opportunities with discipline and our cash position allows us to pursue them without raising new capital or taking on debt. We do not currently have a dividend and buyback program in place, but our balance sheet gives us the flexibility to introduce one when timing and conditions are right. We continue to refine our capital allocation plan, and we'll update investors as it develops. With this, we conclude our prepared remarks. Thank you very much for joining us today.

Operator: This concludes today's conference call. Thank you all for participating. You may now disconnect your lines. Thank you.

#3085. I’ve tested countless Linux distros, and Pond is unlike anything I’ve tried – here’s why

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Linux

Feeling adventurous? This Linux distribution is exciting, efficient and totally unique.

Linux is all about choice. From the kernel all the way up to the desktop environment, you get to determine what is used and even how it is used. The staggering number of distributions, desktops, package managers, file managers, and terminal apps provide you with a nearly infinite combination of choices. That choice is and has always been a key aspect of Linux.

Also: My favorite Linux desktop environment for laptops surprised even me

So too is innovation. If there’s one thing that separates Linux from all other operating systems, it’s the willingness to try something different. Linux developers are always pushing the limits of what an operating system is, and this new take on the OS is the epitome of that.

The distribution in question is called Pond. According to the developers, “Pond is an opportunity for us to play with familiar conventions and experiment with new ideas that make a computer more natural and satisfying.”

The developers have achieved something special. Pond takes the standard UI and turns it on its head. Part tiling window manager, part mobile UI, part GNOME, and part something we’ve never before seen, this desktop environment is special. It took me all of five minutes to fall in love with what they’ve created.

Also: The only 4 Linux email clients I recommend

If you’ve ever considered using a tiling window manager, but thought the lack of a mouse made it seem a bit too complicated, Pond is exactly what you want. Here’s how it works:

Pond uses the Niri window manager to arrange windows in columns along an infinite strip from left to right. In multi-monitor setups, each display gets its own strip, so windows never “overflow” from one monitor to the next.

Also: How to install Arch Linux without losing your mind

At the same time, workspaces are dynamic, and there’s always a new workspace automatically created to the right of the farthest-right window. The combination of the Pond sidebar and Niri’s way of handling windows makes this UI truly original.

Pond doesn’t have a traditional desktop menu. Instead, you open the launcher (using the Super+Space key combination), type the name of the app you want to install, and hit Enter when the app name appears on both the display and as an icon in the top portion of the sidebar.

Another thing that sets Pond apart is how you install apps. Yes, you can open a terminal window and install an app using the pacman command, or you can open the launcher, type install, press Enter, and then type the name of the app you want to install. For instance, if you wanted to install LibreOffice, you would type:

Once you hit Enter a second time, the installation will begin. Many apps install via Flatpak, but on the off-chance an app must be installed via the pacman package manager, you’ll be prompted to type your user password before the installation begins.

As I hinted earlier, Pond is based on Arch Linux, which means it’s a rolling-release distribution. One issue that did give me pause was the lack of a GUI update system, which indicates that updates would have to happen in the terminal, like so:

I installed the Shelly GUI frontend, which does have an update component. Personally, I would simply open the terminal window, type sudo pacman -Syu, hit Enter, and let the update run in the background. But if a GUI is your jam, Shelly is what you want.

Also: A super fast distro for anyone ready to move beyond beginner Linux

It would be sweet if the developers allowed updating the system from within the launcher, so it didn’t require opening the terminal first. The Pond launcher does allow running system commands from the launcher, which will then open the terminal window and execute the command. For instance, open the terminal, type a command, hit Enter, and then scroll through the list of available commands that can be run.

Pond ships with kernel 7.3.4-3, so it has outstanding hardware recognition and performance.

You should definitely give Pond a try, especially if you’re adventurous and want to experience something completely different. If, on the other hand, different is not in your stream, then Pond will frustrate you to no end.

Also: Why Nextcloud Office is my new favorite free productivity suite

Pond excited me more than any OS has in a very long time; so much so that I could see this becoming my go-to OS, once it reaches stable release. Until then, I will keep Pond installed on a laptop, keep upgrading, and see what happens next.

Kudos to the Pond OS team for coming up with something truly unique in an already competitive world.

#3084. An Unsecured Database Exposed About 2 Billion Login Records

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Services & Software > Cybersecurity

The files included passwords and data that can keep you signed in. The number of people affected is unknown.

A database containing about 2 billion login records for sites across the internet was accessible online without a password, security researcher Jeremiah Fowler said in a report published Tuesday by ExpressVPN. The collection included usernames and passwords tied to email, social media, shopping and financial services. Among the files was an ad offering access to email accounts sorted by geography.

The 2 billion figure is an estimate and not representative of the number of people affected, since some accounts may appear more than once and one person can have dozens of logins saved on a single device. Fowler reported the database to its hosting provider, which restricted public access several days later. It’s unclear how long the files had been exposed or who else may have accessed them.

Fowler’s estimate of about 2 billion login records applies to the database he found. Wired put the total at more than 3.5 billion by including a separate database that security firm UpGuard disclosed last week. That database held about 1.64 billion records, including Chinese national ID numbers, phone numbers and school enrollment records.

Some of the files Fowler reviewed appeared to be from infostealers — malicious software that collects saved passwords and other data from infected devices. Once that information is collected, brokers can buy it in bulk, sort it by country or account type and resell it in smaller batches. A buyer interested in email accounts in a particular country can pay for that slice of the data. The people selling it can make money from the same records more than once.

Fowler saw signs that the files came from multiple sources, but couldn’t determine who assembled the collection or whether it was used for sales, research or another purpose.

I saw a version of that business in my reporting on the dark web for CNET. On Genesis Market, buyers could shop for stolen accounts by location and category, including banking, email and social media. By the time authorities disrupted the marketplace in 2023, it had offered access to data from more than 1.5 million compromised computers, according to the Justice Department.

You can look up your email address in Have I Been Pwned to see whether it appears in a known data exposure. A clean result only tells you what’s in the service’s index.

If you see an unfamiliar login or suspect your device is infected, use a different, trusted device to change the affected password and sign out of other sessions. Start with your email if several accounts may be affected, since that’s where password reset links often go. Replace reused passwords with unique ones, use a password manager to keep track of them and turn on two-factor authentication where it’s available.

Identity theft protection services monitor for signs that your personal information has been exposed or misused. In a leak like this one, an alert about an exposed password can tell you which account to secure, especially if you’ve reused that password elsewhere. Aura is one of the services we tested for CNET’s guide to the best identity theft protection services.

Warning: may cause (friendly) arguments!

Few board games come close to being as great as this one. Catan is a highly addictive strategy game for three to four players which turns you into hard-nosed settlers, competing to conquer an island. You must collect resource cards to build roads, village and cities, but collecting them heavily relies on dice rolls and trading with other players. Oh, and there's a resource-stealing robber too to spice things up, so watch out!

When we're having a cozy date night, P for Pizza is a game my partner and I always play. In this fast-paced card game, you have to shout out a word that links the letter on one card to the category on another (on a pile in the middle of the table). For example, a food that starts with G, an actress whose name begins with K, a stringed instrument that starts with S, and so on. You need to be quick to add a slice to your pile, and the first one to form a 'pizza slice' wins.

Need a party game for the holidays? Try Herd Mentality. It's easy to pick up and play as all you need to do is flip a card and read out a random question like, "Who is the most popular female artist of all time?" You and the other players then write down the answer you think will be the most common among the group. If you're in the majority, you win points; if not, you'll be left with the dreaded pink cow of doom. And as someone who adores cows, you don't want to get stuck with this one...

If you want a fast-paced board/card game where you deduce your fellow players' behavior, The Chameleon is for you. In this game, everyone know a secret word except one hidden imposter. Each player gives a single related clue to prove they belong without revealing too much. The group then votes to unmask the traitor... or Chameleon, if you will. Each round can last as long as the group likes.

The first time I played You Can't Say UMM was at a board games café with my friends. We laughed so much that our jaws hurt and we had tears running down our faces. In this card game, you have to describe an object to your teammate without saying "Umm" or "Err." The opposing team can catch you out and penalize you. Opponents can also add "rules" to your turn, such as, "Swap seats with a teammate after every correct guess." It's harder than it sounds, and it's a barrel of laughs.

Cards Against Humanity is the perfect card game for adults — and to determine who among your friend group has the darkest humor. One player reads a fill-in-the-blank prompt from a black card, and everyone else submits their funniest, most offensive, or absurd white answer card. The reader picks the winner, awarding a point. It can get really horrible really fast — but it's oh so fun.

My partner and I play Ransom Notes with our friends fairly often. In this game, you and the other players race against a timer to answer outrageous prompts using only a limited handful of random word magnets. Everyone reads their grammatically chaotic sentences aloud while a rotating judge picks the funniest response to award a point. The first to five points (or the number of your choosing) wins!

#3082. Readdle’s Documents app adds voice recording with transcripts, summaries, more

Readdle updated its Documents app for iPhone and iPad this week with Voice Notes, a new AI-powered feature that lets users record conversations and automatically generate transcripts, summaries, and follow-up notes. Here are the details.

While the habit of recording meetings, lectures, or even one’s own thoughts is not particularly new, modern AI tools and models have made it considerably easier to extract useful information from these recordings without having to listen back to them in their entirety or take copious notes that can distract from the actual conversation.

This week, Readdle’s Documents introduced Voice Notes, which “lets you record audio and turn it into a summary, follow-ups, and a full transcript,” as the company put it.

Users can start a new recording session by tapping the “+” button in the app and selecting Voice Notes. Alternatively, they can start recording from the iPhone’s Action button, which is a nice touch.

Once they’re done, Readdle says Documents can generate:

Users can cycle through these three tabs, where they can also listen to the original recording or copy and share the information.

Readdle says Voice Notes can recognize multiple languages in the same conversation, with the actual transcript preserving the languages as spoken, “while the summary and follow-ups are generated in the most frequently spoken language.”

Each voice note is saved as a single file in Documents that contains the original recording, transcript, summary, and follow-ups. Users can organize these files into folders, share them, sync them with their cloud storage, and save the transcript as a separate .txt file.

However, if users give a voice note’s AI-generated content a thumbs down, Readdle may retain its transcript and summary for up to six months, or until the user objects to their processing, whichever comes first.

The company also says user data isn’t used to train AI models, although third-party AI providers may retain inputs for up to 30 days for abuse and misuse monitoring, or longer if required by law.

#3081. Nvidia Is Also Trying to Fix the Bug Causing Excessive SSD Writing

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Tech > Computing > Computer Accessories > Components > Graphic cards

Nvidia has issued software updates, but it's unclear if the problem is completely fixed.

Nvidia has had its share of drama lately, with the ousting and sudden un-ousting of CEO Jensen Huang after it was discovered he’d had multiple affairs, including one that involved an alleged member of a Chinese spy network. The fallout from the revelations was so significant that some worried Huang’s fate could be a major disruptor to the health of international markets and the future of the entire AI industry.

Given that, the world’s largest semiconductor company possibly wishes its biggest problem were software-related. But that won’t be much comfort to PC users affected by a software bug in Nvidia’s graphics driver that has caused some to experience excessive writes to their solid-state drives.

The issue began popping up in mid-November as posts on Nvidia’s support forums, as well as on Reddit and sites like HardForum, reported seeing as much as 30GB to 70GB of data per hour written to their SSDs. These types of drives wear down quickly over months of such use.

Nvidia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment and hasn’t made any public statements on the issue, but did acknowledge it in a hotfix and subsequent software update for its Windows 11 GeForce Game Ready Driver 621.40, where it said under Fixed General Bugs, “Excessive writes to file nvlog.nvlgstg may occur in background.” The driver that appeared to have caused the problems was released on Nov. 12.Some tech experts on social media had been suggesting rolling back to older graphics drivers before the hotfixes were released and warned that letting the problem go unchecked could cause an SSD to eventually fail.

Described by WCCF Tech as “a hotfix for the hotfix,” the new update appears to fix the issue in ways that the previous fix did not.

Nvidia’s software problem closely mirrors an issue AMD had with its own Adrenalin Edition graphics software just weeks ago. As of Nov. 18, AMD was still making tweaks to its graphics software to iron out any lingering problems.

PCGamer offered a way to check if your PC is affected by the excess writing issue.

Open Task Manager, click on the Details tab and right-click on the columns at the top to select “I/O write bytes” as one of your Task Manager columns. By doing that, you can see if the file “NVDisplay.Container.exe” is writing a huge amount of data to your data drive.

If that’s the case, you should update immediately to Nvidia’s latest drivers for the fix. In fact, it might be a good idea to update whether you’re experiencing high write rates or not, just to be safe.

#3080. Meta Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not the worst of it

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

According to a Reuters investigation, Meta employees testing Muse said the agent messaged them about topics they hadn’t asked it about, including career advice, a follow-up on a request for childcare, products they hadn’t purchased, and, crucially, bank account balances they didn’t recognize.

These incidents “prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data,” Reuters said.

Reuters said “an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: ‘BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2,722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5,899.57.'” In another instance, Muse booked a non-refundable Airbnb for an employee who hadn’t instructed it to.

Muse notified another employee, who was using the agent on her personal phone, about a message she’d received on Signal, though she said she hadn’t given the agent access to the encrypted messaging app.

Reuters and the AI Now Institute determined, through testing on an Android phone and a Mac, that Muse used “permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.” Because Muse is set up with automatic access to Android push notifications, it didn’t need explicit app access to read messages.

The tests did not work on an iPhone, suggesting better protections against Muse’s prying.

Similarly, in September, a user reported Muse had shared his address with a Facebook Marketplace buyer before checking with him. The incident was ultimately a misunderstanding between the terms the user thought he’d consented to and how much access he was actually handing over, which exemplifies that Meta and the user may have explicitly different definitions of access, and that Muse can take advantage of that grey area.

Meta told Reuters these incidents were either isolated or the result of hallucinations, though Reuters could not confirm that.

#3078. Anthropic Is Down 7% Since Its IPO. History Says a $5,000 Investment Could Be Worth This Much in a Year.

By Jennifer Saibil – Nov 26, 2026 at 10:13AM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) made history last week when it went public in the largest initial public offering (IPO) ever. But so far, the stock isn't moving in the direction shareholders would hope for. The stock, which went public at $83 per share, opened its first day of trading at $111.50, and closed it at $97.17, has fallen to $77.40 as of this writing. That’s a 7% drop from the IPO price, and a much steeper one from the prices that retail investors could get on Day 1.

But things can change quickly in the stock market, and a year from now, Anthropic could be much higher -- or much lower. Let's consider what a $5,000 investment in Anthropic stock might be worth in a year.

The theory behind the bull case for Anthropic is that its Claude artificial intelligence (AI) model will be integrated into businesses everywhere. As of now, it already has 11,900 customers paying it at least $100,000 annually, including 250 customers with annual spending of more than $10 million. Widespread enterprise adoption of Claude could lead to a state where it's simply viewed as a necessary part of business operations; that would generate incredible growth at Anthropic.

The company’s most recent results have been phenomenal. Trailing-12-month revenue increased 1,200% year over year in the third quarter, and if it continues to demonstrate such staggering growth, it could quickly become one of the largest companies in the world by sales. It would also become profitable at scale, and its vast investments in compute power — which it has been gobbling up from a roster of top AI infrastructure providers such as Amazon (AMZN -3.12%), Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%)(GOOGL -2.13%), and Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +1.30%)— would yield results. It has spending agreements with these companies and others to the tune of around $900 billion, with deals extending into 2036.

Management sees vast use cases for its technology. It envisions AI helping to end poverty and cure disease as well as drive economic growth.

AI is definitely heating up, but it may not offer long-term growth in quite the way Anthropic imagines. To begin with, there are already many competitors offering foundation models, and as the technology changes, there could be more. The market is already forgetting how AI stocks tumbled when the Chinese-developed model Deepseek came onto the scene last year. There's no reason to believe other things like that can't happen. Anthropic itself is an extremely young company, and it only launched Claude in 2023, pulling market share from OpenAI's ChatGPT.

IPO stocks tend to have bumpy rides early on, and given Anthropic's high price-to-sales multiple of 29, the stock has considerable room to drop if the company’s growth slows down. Wall Street expects its revenue to increase by 137% in 2027 — but that would be a major deceleration. If that forecast proves accurate, the market may conclude that Anthropic isn’t worth such a lofty sales multiple. If its top-line growth meets Wall Street's expectations, revenue would be about $83 billion. But if its P/S ratio gets cut in half to 14, its market cap would be $1.16 trillion. That's a 16% increase from today's value, turning a $5,000 investment made now into a position worth about $5,800.

#3077. This Is What My Apple Watch Heard When I Let It Evesdrop on My Conversations

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

No, your phone isn’t listening to you. But what about your Apple Watch? I’ve been testing new Audio Intelligence features that record conversations around me, and despite how disturbing it may sound to have your smartwatch listening and taking notes of your entire day, the reality has been a lot more mundane.

Along with the general sensor, processor, and battery upgrades, the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 introduced Audio Intelligence, a new set of features that allows the watch to listen in on conversations.

Siri Recap generates summaries of what you’ve discussed throughout the day, while Live Rewind gives you a transcript of the last 15 seconds of audio in case you missed something.

It’s similar functionality as AI-powered recording pins like Plaud or Amazon’s Bee, but within the context of your smartwatch and without the additional cost or subscription.

And it’s completely optional. You have to first opt-in to the features to activate them, then choose to turn the feature you want on whenever you want to start using it. Then you can leave it on all day, set it on a schedule or toggle it manually whenever you need it. If you’re like me and forget that it’s on, you get reminders that it’s still listening or to check your recaps.

The fact that you have so much control over whether you use it and how much helped ease the creepy factor for me, but there’s still everyone else to consider.

Beyond a barely audible chime when I double-click the Digital Crown to activate Live Rewind, there’s no way to alert others that the feature is in use and that whoever’s in earshot is inadvertently getting roped into my little experiment as well. Other wearables like smart glasses have an indicator light on the front to alert spectators when they’re recording video.

I’ve been testing Audio Intelligence in the WatchOS 27.3 (and iOS) public beta for two weeks. Because this isn’t the final version (Apple says it will release publicly later this year), consider this a sneak preview.

Let’s get Live Rewind out of the way because there’s not a lot to say about it. Whether from a lack of muscle memory (or usefulness), I’ve had to go out of my way to remember the feature exists.

I figured it’d come in handy for those “come again?” moments during conversations, but the reality is that it’s just easier to ask someone to repeat what they said than remember to double-press the Digital Crown at just the right moment. I can see it being more useful when you’re listening to a presentation or other event.

Fifteen seconds go by a lot faster than I expect and by the time I realize something might be worth revisiting, the person has moved on with the conversation. I either missed what I intended to get or just captured the silence after.

Siri Recap has been more useful, though it’s still hit-or-miss. The feature gives you high-level summaries of what it heard — it doesn’t provide a transcript to review, and it doesn’t identify who said what. It shines brightest during dedicated meetings when there’s a single conversation to follow rather than a jumble of unrelated discussions.

One success story: I was moderating the chat for our iPhone Duo live folding test on YouTube while Matthew Murray, CNET’s lab director, answered viewer questions on the stream.

I thought I’d caught the gist of what he was saying, but the typing must’ve distracted me more than I realized because I was pleasantly surprised to learn some interesting facts that I’d missed in the Siri Recap, like “Opening a phone 20 times daily over 10 years equals 73,000 folds” or that the “machine runs approximately 22,560 cycles every 24 hours”.

But Siri’s batting average wasn’t always that good, which made it challenging to trust the notes. During a conversation with another mom about car-pool logistics, Siri Recap pulled out action items, like who I was picking up and at what time, which I appreciated, but the information wasn’t accurate. Not only had Siri gotten the names of the kids wrong, it also had me picking up the wrong kid. Clearly, the mental load of figuring out after-school logistics is challenging even for Siri.

Siri can’t handle the messy conversations (and TV shows)

Where things get interesting (and occasionally hilarious) is how Siri discerns what constitutes a conversation and how many topics belong in a single recap.

Siri is generally good at accurately labeling what conversations are about: “Parent-teacher conferences,” “Car-pool logistics,” “Folding phone durability testing.” But rather than keeping them separate, as it should, it sometimes conflates two or even three completely unrelated conversations into a single recap.

I encountered bullet points summarizing a serious conversation with a friend about a medical condition alongside notes about a chaotic (albeit funny) exploding apple cider incident with my kids. The two conversations happened within the same two-hour window, but they were by no means back-to-back.

It’s a good thing Siri Recap leaves out tone and volume cause that last bullet would’ve been in ALL CAPS.

What it did decide was worthy of a standalone recap was a discussion about wedding plans during an episode of Nobody Wants This on Netflix. To be fair, this would’ve absolutely warranted a recap if I’d been discussing my own wedding plans; however, the fact that the “conversation” happened at midnight should’ve tipped off Siri that this was a late-night binge session and not an actual conversation needing to be recapped.

Rather than coming away better informed about the important conversations I’d had throughout the day, I came away feeling validated by the sheer chaos of it all. The constant whiplash of being pulled in a dozen different directions — bouncing between work, kids, gossip and the occasional sticky beverage crisis — was real and now immortalized (until the recap automatically expires if you don’t choose to save it).

For now, while novel, neither Siri Recap nor Live Rewind is reason enough to buy (or avoid) the Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4. They’re two of our top-rated smartwatches for their fitness, health and other smart features. Audio Intelligence is either an added bonus (it’s free) or something you can ignore altogether.

But if you do decide to venture into this brave new world of AI notetakers, my suggestion would be to use Siri Recap intentionally rather than leaving it running all day.

Turn it on before a work meeting, a doctor’s appointment or another conversation where you might want a few notes to jog your memory later. Just make sure everyone involved knows it’s enabled and is comfortable with it, and that you’re not relying on it for crucial information.

If the stakes are high, have a backup — whether that’s your own notes or a recording — lest you risk coming home with the wrong kid.

I tested the viral Ohuhu markers and they smashed my expectations

If you’re an artist and you use social media, you’ve probably heard about Ohuhu by now. This brand quickly made a name for itself simply because they offered high-quality alcohol based markers at prices that undercut competitors. I have to admit that I turned my nose up at them at first; I didn’t believe they could be as good as the markers I already owned when they cost so much less.

In short, I should have listened to Ohuhu’s supporters. I was able to try out both the Honolulu 2S alcohol markers, and my first ever set of acrylics with the Hilo brush tip acrylic paint markers. I was blown away by both.

I started off with the Hilo acrylic markers. These markers have a single, soft and flexible brush tip, and you can currently get either a set of 48 or a set of 72 at Amazon. As soon as the pen touched the page, I was immediately struck by the vibrancy of the colors and the opacity of the ink. And compared to other name brand acrylic markers, they’re significantly cheaper — the 72 set works out to around 70 cents per marker at the Black Friday sale price.

There are some downsides to contend with. When it came to coloring small, detailed areas... I pretty much had to forget about staying within the lines. I struggled to achieve fine pointed shapes and found that the ink pooled into circular shapes every time I attempted them. I also had issues with streaky ink, and my coloring paper pilled in certain spots, too.

This is my first time using acrylic markers, so I’m willing to acknowledge all these problems could come down to my lack of skills. I’m going to keep using them and see if I can improve my technique and layer up more to combat the streaks. The pilling probably isn’t going away until I get a coloring book with higher quality paper, though.

Next up, I tried the Honolulu 2S alcohol based markers. You get more color options here as the sets come in packs of 24 all the way up to 320; and these markers have a dual tip. One side has a brush tip, and the other is a chisel tip.

Compared to the Hilo's, the Honolulu 2S’s brush tip is firmer and stiffer. Even though the Hilo brush tip felt great, I liked the Honolulu 2S’s firmer brush tip even more, and found it easier to control when coloring detailed areas and sharp points. It still handles curves just as well, and the chisel tip comes in handy for filling large areas too. I fell in love with alcohol-based markers years back because they produce a beautiful, non-streaky finish. The Honolulu 2S markers absolutely live up to that and looked fantastic on the page.

However, using alcohol based inks comes with more of a learning curve. I started off filling in a large black area on the page once again, and was very impressed that the marker didn’t bleed much at all. However, other colors like the dark blue and gray didn’t fare so well, and bled right over the lines.

The bleed can be mitigated by using paper made specifically for alcohol markers, but you don’t have that option if you want to color in a specific coloring book. It took an hour or two for me to get used to it, but I eventually learned to leave plenty of space while filling areas in to account for the bleed.

As well as bleeding over the lines, I also had to watch out for the ink bleeding through the paper — Ohuhu provides a plastic sheet to place under your work to avoid staining the next page in your sketchbook. The ink in the Honolulu 2S markers was clearly visible on the back side of the paper I colored on (seen on the left of the image below,) but none got through to the next page. Meanwhile, the back side of the page I colored with the Hilo markers (seen on the right below) was completely clean.

If you’re a budding artist, I highly recommend picking up a set of Ohuhu markers. The Hilo acrylic markers are the ones for you if you want the most vibrancy, and are also great if you want to have the option to redo areas if you’re not happy with them. Meanwhile, the Honolulu 2S markers stand out for their enormous color selection, excellent brush tip and super-smooth finish.

These markers are cheaper than the big brands, and are even better value when discounted. Grab them while you can!

#3073. Can AI plan terrorist attacks? The US tested ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Investigators tried to bypass AI safeguards to generate plans. The results exposed security gaps and raised questions about preventing misuse.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO) conducted a series of tests earlier this year designed to determine whether users could bypass guardrails and convince AIs to plan terrorist attacks. The investigators succeeded. In October, the agency published a report titled “Covert Testing Used Common Platforms to Create Viable Attack Plans,” which was released to the public in November.

The tests were conducted using Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, and Grok. All four AIs produced attack scenarios that subject matter experts were able to confirm would have mostly succeeded.

I spoke via email with the report’s lead author, Kevin Walsh, director of IT and cybersecurity audits at the GAO. He told ZDNET:

In general, the details provided by the four AI platforms are not novel. Much of the information is readily available on the internet. But these plans were generated in hours, rather than weeks or months. AI could also surface ideas or methods that may not have been previously considered.

To the companies’ credit, their safeguards have continued to evolve since we conducted these tests. The companies also assure us that this is an area of concern and ongoing research. However, our report concludes that, in its current state, this technology can be dangerous, and its misuse represents a growing risk to our nation.

The Government Accountability Office is an independent, nonpartisan agency that works for the legislative branch of the US government. Its responsibility is to “examine how taxpayer dollars are spent and provide Congress and federal agencies with objective, non-partisan, fact-based information to help the government save money and work more efficiently.”

Also: Why enterprise AI agents could become the ultimate insider threat

The GAO investigators constructed two attack scenarios: detonating an explosive device for maximum damage and destroying an electrical grid substation for maximum disruption. They randomly split the challenge across the four AI platforms, so that two AIs each worked independently on the explosive challenge while two others worked independently on the substation challenge.

This assignment split is where, after being shown the results, the AI companies pushed back. That seems justifiable. By not giving all four AI services the same set of assignments, the GAO lost the ability to objectively measure all four against each other.

As a platform-vs-platform comparison, the GAO investigation falls short. But as an investigation into whether the generative AI tools available in mid-2026 might be able to be used for credible national security threats, its results are definitive. The investigation also highlighted how AIs reduce the time and effort involved in researching how such attacks might be carried out.

While the four AIs used for the tests were identified in the report, the GAO did not publish which AIs were used to carry out which tests. Instead, “Due to the sensitive nature and content of the testing, we randomly assigned an alphabetic character to each platform for purposes of presenting the test results within this report.”

For the bomb-damage scenario, the two assigned AIs recommended different approaches, although both provided specific actionable steps in order to accomplish the tasks.

Platform A constructed a scenario where an IED (improvised explosive device) would be detonated inside a hotel parking structure. It provided a timetable for when the hotel was expected to be crowded due to a public event as well as where the hotel’s security was likely to be weakest.

It recommended where to rent a van from outside the city, how to disable the GPS in the van, a shopping list of supplies used in constructing the device, specific stores to shop at, where to park the van in the garage, how to set up the device for detonation, and even a bus route to take in order to get back to the attacker’s personal car.

Also: Could cyberwar knock us back to the Stone Age?

After additional prompting by GAO investigators, Platform A “also generated an image that directed us to a specific area to deploy the IED to cause significant damage to the location. Specifically, Platform A generated an image of a parking structure that recommended where to park the vehicle.”

GAO investigators verified the plan’s viability by consulting with a bomb squad commander at a big-city fire department. The bomb tech confirmed that following the instructions with the recommended components would result in an explosion. The GAO also confirmed the availability of the supplies from the vendors the AI recommended.

Platform B targeted a convention center. Its recommended preparations were extensive. It recommended incorporating a shell company as a cover story so that the attacker could legitimately lease a secure, ventilated barn. It recommended a rural purchasing circuit, buying just enough supplies at four rural co-ops over four days in order to avoid triggering any mandatory reporting requirements.

The AI then recommended purchasing diesel fuel from three truck stops using cash, making “unremarkable purchases at unremarkable locations.” The AI recommended transferring the fuel into sealed 55-gallon drums at the barn. It also recommended careful storage conditions, including temperature, drum integrity, and separation from other materials (the materials themselves were redacted from the GAO’s report).

Also: Apple, Google, and Microsoft join Anthropic’s Project Glasswing to defend world’s most critical software

Next up, the AI recommended a communications security review, burner phones, varied procurement routes, and information compartmentalization. It recommended taking a taxi to a waterfront and then walking south for 40 minutes. It suggested confirming sight lines and contractor access to road positions. It even suggested that while the attacker’s face would appear on three cameras, the footage from those specific cameras would not be reviewed for three weeks.

It then recommended sending decoy trucks into the target, then sneaking an explosive vehicle into a parking garage.

When the GAO reviewed the recommendations, the agency discovered the AI got event dates wrong. However, according to the bomb squad commander, the components and procedures recommended would definitely have resulted in an explosion.

As with the bomb-damage scenario, the two AIs participating in the electrical grid scenario took different approaches, but both had the potential to be disturbingly effective.

Platform C began by identifying electrical substations where an attack could be most effective. It produced a list that helped identify vulnerable substations. After some prompting, “The platform then selected a substation in a specific major U.S. city and estimated that the loss of power would cause billions of dollars in damages.”

It identified the specific location on the specified substation where a drone could hit and cause a short circuit, which would destroy a key component. It actually provided a simulated video of the drone attack as well as a diagram that showed the component’s failure process.

The AI identified the exact model of the drone that it felt was best suited for the attack. Initially, the AI’s guardrails refused to provide an exact location for a target substation. That said, “The platform eventually provided the name of a substation, which we used to identify an exact location.”

The day after the AI made its recommendations, the GAO reported, “We observed that the platform had removed portions of our chat discussions that related to electrical grid vulnerabilities. It is unclear whether this action was initiated as part of a guardrail or if by error.” After two weeks, the account had not been suspended.

GAO investigators confirmed that the suggested drone model did exist, the route to the target was accurate, and the proposed target did exist. A subject matter expert consulted by the GAO “Verified that the information provided by Platform C was generally correct. The expert stated such an attack could, at the very least, cause damage to the substation. However, the expert could not confirm whether the specific drone suggested by Platform C would cause a short circuit or destruction of the substation.”

After rented vans, shell companies, and aerial drone attacks, Platform D decided to do it old school: plain old firearms. Point. Shoot. Buh-bye.

The AI provided GAO investigators with a primary target substation along with three secondary backup locations. It recommended locations near a large international airport and a bunch of data centers to increase the economic impact from the attack. And just in case it wasn’t clear enough, the AI drew a map highlighting the locations of the target substations.

It recommended the use of a gun, recommended the type of weapon along with the proper ammo in order to maximize the effects of the attack, along with where an attacker could go to procure such weapons. It recommended both online and in-person surveillance of the target locations prior to initiating an attack.

As with Platform C’s recommendation, Platform D recommended specific components in the substation that would be most vulnerable to an attack. It even provided images highlighting where the transformers would be most vulnerable.

The GAO report stated that the AI originally threw up guardrails and refused to provide the information requested, saying, “Our query raised serious concerns about potential intent to engage in criminal activity or harm critical infrastructure due to the context of the conversation.”

Also: AI finds zero-day flaws for just $4 now – even mediocre hackers can cash in

The more telling comment is this from the report: “However, the platform ultimately provided us with information needed for an attack.” I’m thinking someone in the GAO could probably sell water to a fish.

As with Platform C, GAO noted that the AI removed some of the chat content from the chat history. As for whether the plan would work, “We verified the planned attack was viable for half of the substation locations recommended by Platform D.”

A subject matter expert also confirmed that attacking the specific areas of the transformers recommended could cause an outage and that the specific firearms and ammunition recommended were available from the purchase locations specified. The AI did make an error in the generated maps by incorrectly placing roads.

But of the four recommended locations, two were actually viable. GAO investigators took a field trip to the recommended locations and verified that two could work for such an attack, but the other two had high walls that obscured the view of the targets.

After completing the tests, the GAO investigators presented the results to the AI vendors and gave the companies the opportunity to respond. While the GAO report purposely hid which AI provided which attack plan, the report is fully forthcoming with the complete response letters from each company.

In reading the responses, I found the difference in attitudes and approach to the question most interesting.

Anthropic’s four-page response letter was signed by Anthony Cimino, head of federal affairs. The company’s response was courteous but strongly challenging. It moved immediately from thanking the GAO to questioning the statistical significance and criticizing the absence of a control group.

Anthropic’s letter about Claude says, “We ask that the report specify that there were not enough trials to achieve significance, and that therefore any conclusions are at most preliminary.”

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac

Google’s three-page response about Gemini was unsigned. The majority of the response discussed launch reviews, executive oversight, Google’s testing, filters, training, and human review practices. The company did agree that Gemini could violate guidelines. It was the most disengaged from the GAO’s report, and it offered little in the way of explanation about the issues raised.

Google’s letter says, “We have deep respect for the mission of the Government Accountability Office and we want to underscore that Google takes your work very seriously.”

OpenAI’s three-page response letter about ChatGPT was signed by Chan Park, head of US and Canada policy and partnerships. It says the company reviewed 325 responses from the AI and identified three that fell short of how the AI is supposed to behave. The company apparently replayed the requests and said that it was unable to reproduce the responses reported by the GAO.

OpenAI was the clearest in stating that the GAO’s results demonstrated unacceptable behavior from the AI, stating: “Even a discrete contribution to a broader harmful activity can matter, and improving safeguards against such assistance remains an ongoing priority.”

SpaceXAI’s 363-word, less-than-a-page response about Grok was unsigned. The company emphasized how much effort was required to bypass the safeguards and mentioned that there have been improvements in the guardrails since the GAO conducted its tests earlier that year.

Then we reach the “Say what, now?” moment of our day.

The company replied, “It is worth noting that GAO received its output from paid accounts in the United States. SpaceXAl provides unique moderation policies for registered, paid US account holders that reflect the lower risk profile of such accounts compared to free or foreign accounts.”

In other words, the company contends that paying US account holders have a lower risk profile than free or foreign users, and that therefore Grok provides fewer guardrails. The letter provides no supporting evidence for that assumption.

While a credit card number could provide some linkage to a user’s identity compared to fully free accounts, users could easily obtain a prepaid card that allows for completely anonymous paid usage. I just think that making an assumption about risk factor based on whether a user is willing to pay $8 a month is a particularly fallacious security policy.

The GAO report is clear that each of the AIs did provide some pushback against providing cookbooks for conducting the destructive behavior.

The agency conducted a number of adversarial prompt seeding operations, including roleplaying, special encoding, character transformation, word transformation, separating intent from content, taking very small baby steps in prompting, and other approaches often used to convince an AI to effectively “jailbreak” its guardrails.

Also: If you’re not working on quantum-safe encryption now, it’s already too late

While the AIs were eventually persuaded to participate in guiding attacks, some accounts were later shut down by the AI platforms, indicating that while the guardrails didn’t prevent the AI from providing initial advice, they were eventually flagged and terminated.

While that’s a bit of “locking the barn door after the horse has bolted,” it does indicate that the AI vendors are working toward more comprehensive protections.

The GAO report didn’t address the larger issue of whether censoring the AIs is ultimately in society’s best interest.

As a counterterrorism and infrastructure security professional, I often think of Ben Franklin’s famous statement, “Those who would give up essential Liberty, to purchase a little temporary Safety, deserve neither Liberty nor Safety.” Old Ben never had to contend with nukes, cyberattacks, and machines smarter than he was.

Personally, I lament the need for guardrails because they limit potentially legitimate access to information. But as the GAO’s scenario shows, strong guardrails are ultimately necessary, not because of the AIs, but because we humans are our own worst enemy.

Also: Rogue AI incidents hit ‘tens of thousands’: Can businesses trust these tools?

On the other hand, it’s not as if humans haven’t been able to figure out how to conduct violent acts all on their own, without the help of an AI. For example, the Anarchist’s Cookbook, which is essentially a recipe book for the home manufacture of explosives and illicit drugs, has been publicly available continuously since the early 1970s. While also outdated, Amazon even sells a reprinted 1941 manual about the chemistry of powder and explosives.

So, while it is definitely disturbing that the AIs could, collectively, provide four unique attack plans for civic disruption, they are not opening a door previously unavailable to those with nefarious intent. I laud the GAO for providing additional testing feedback to the AI companies, and the AI companies for improving their guardrails.

But while the report is scary in that all that information was presented in an organized manner by each of the AIs, that availability doesn’t bestow a new superpower on crackpots. After all, AIs are trained on publicly available information.

One of the more costly, but necessary, tradeoffs of an open society is that all this information is available. Whether an AI is used to structure that information is largely irrelevant in the face of that simple fact.

#3072. Zelda Producers: Ocarina of Time Remake Is a Bridge to the Future

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Nintendo’s execs on how young designers reinterpreted a classic game, maximized the Switch 2’s graphics capabilities and briefly considered turning the Joy-Con into an ocarina.

Over the last month, I fell in love with a new game that’s actually old. It’s happened to me before, but Nintendo’s Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake drove that feeling home in a surprising way. How did Nintendo get me to fall so deeply in love again with a game I’ve already played? And why is it still winning me over, even with Grand Theft Auto 6 here?

I’m still thinking about (and playing) Ocarina of Time on the Switch 2, even with GTA 6 loaded up at home. GTA’s universe overwhelms me, but it also makes me appreciate Ocarina’s focus and clarity. And it’s also another incredible graphics showcase for what the Switch 2 is capable of. Yes, GTA 6 is jaw-dropping. But so are Ocarina’s 60fps vistas and details. Zelda pioneered 3D gaming before GTA ever went 3D.

I also can’t stop thinking about what a game like this means for Nintendo’s next wave of Switch 2 games, and a future Zelda game. Zelda’s previous games became increasingly open world, full of multiplying tasks and larger maps. It can get overwhelming. Ocarina of Time’s focus is smaller, but still tangled and immersive. Can the two concepts feed off each other? Will Ocarina help rethink where the next Zeldas are heading? And, maybe, where other open-world games are heading, too?

At Ocarina’s launch, I met in person with Nintendo’s producers for the remake, Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, to discuss what it all meant and how the remake bridged the gap between the “old Zelda” and “new Zelda.” Aonuma has been a producer for Zelda games since the original Ocarina of Time, and Fujibayashi directed both Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom.

For this project, they brought on staffers who’d worked on Tears of the Kingdom, many of them much younger developers.

“In fact, some of them hadn’t even played the original Ocarina of Time on Nintendo 64,” says Aonuma. “We also saw this as a really interesting opportunity for this younger staff to make discoveries on the course of this project that they could bring forward on future Zelda projects that they might work on as well.”

There are a lot more subtle visual clues, I found, even than what I remembered in Nintendo’s last two Zelda games.

“When we were working on Tears of the Kingdom, we had this very high capacity to express all kinds of details and this feeling of immersion in the world, and that’s something I think was a big influence on the remake,” says Aonuma. “Whether it’s a visual detail that you might spot from a distance that you may not have in the original, that could be something that draws the player in and suddenly gives them the motivation to explore.”

What worked wonders, I found, was the quiet, subtle immersion, especially when exploring dungeons or figuring out solutions I’d forgotten decades ago. I had to study the environment for clues.

That’s the magic ingredient: a throughline in the Zelda games that Fujibayashi says is “the idea of exploration and discovery.”

Fujibayashi appreciates how the visual tools have improved, even since Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom on the original Switch.

“A system that lets you share a high, dense volume of information visually provides new ways of giving clues to the player: They can use their sight to gather the information they need to do some of the puzzle solving,” he says. “Even if you compare the graphics to Breath of the Wild, it looks slightly more realistic now. And that impacts how we approach puzzle solving and puzzle creation.”

I think about Grand Theft Auto as the new benchmark for immersion and graphic detail, but I’m also finding that a lot of GTA’s discoveries are made through pop-up interaction graphics that let you know when something can be activated. Ocarina of Time doesn’t always do this. And I also can’t help but wonder: Could the Switch 2 achieve a way to run a new wave of impressive games using optimized graphics, even something on a level like Grand Theft Auto’s latest?

Or, rather, what if Nintendo aims for a new level of hyper-immersion in its games going forward, learning from Ocarina of Time?

Speaking of immersion, I kind of wish I could hold my Joy-Con up and use it like an ocarina in the new game. You can’t, although you can use the controllers to play notes or hum or play a tune into the built-in microphone using your own voice or instrument — something lots of people have been showing off online. But the Joy-Con-as-ocarina idea almost became a reality.

“To be honest, we did briefly think about doing exactly that, but then we also considered how difficult it is to turn the Joy-Con into something that’s going to make a sound that is faithful, and then also how to develop that into the application inside of the game as well,” says Aonuma. “What we ultimately decided to do instead was to have this audio recognition feature in the software where you can use any instrument that you would like, whether it’s analog or digital, and you can play these themes and have the effect in the game and experience that way.”

What I’m really hoping for is a Majora’s Mask remake, the second N64 Zelda game that built off Ocarina’s graphics engine. Nintendo could do the same here, although Nintendo wouldn’t answer my questions about Majora’s Mask during my interview.

I’m still unlocking all the little secrets in Ocarina of Time, sinking into the world as I go. And when I play the notes on my Switch, I imagine I’m playing that ocarina. After playing this Zelda game, I wonder what Nintendo could do with that same level of detail for Mario’s return on the Switch 2, almost 10 years after the last new 3D Mario game on the Switch. We might know the answer to that soon enough.
