#3014. Should You Buy Nvidia After Its Sharp Decline? Warren Buffett’s Long-Held Investment Philosophy Provides a Clear Answer

Is it time to get greedy while others are fearful?

By Adam Levy – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:15PM EST

The past six weeks have been tough for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) and its shareholders. In October, growing concerns about how businesses will finance future build-outs for artificial intelligence (AI) started weighing on semiconductor stocks.

In early November, the mid-term election results showed a clear rebuke of massive data centers and the potential for increased regulations to slow development. And, of course, Jensen Huang's affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees ultimately led to his temporary resignation, leaving Nvidia without a permanent CEO for 11 days.

The end result is a stock well off its all-time high, despite having just reported third-quarter revenue and earnings growth that both exceeded 100%. CFO and interim-CEO Colette Kress said it's "business as usual" at Nvidia, painting an optimistic picture on the company's earnings call. So, with the stock trading at a level rarely seen in the past year, should investors consider buying the stock? Warren Buffett's long-held investment philosophy can provide the answer to that question.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

Many investors might look at Nvidia's drop and think, "The market is fearful; I should get greedy." After all, Kress just increased her guidance for fiscal 2028 revenue growth from 70% to 75%. Wall Street analysts see Nvidia's earnings per share climbing above $16 next year. The stock trades at ridiculously low multiples.

While it's true that Buffett has long noted that one of the keys to his success as an investor is "to be greedy only when others are fearful," that's not the only requirement for a good investment. Buffett also only invested in stocks when he had a high degree of confidence in their future. If a company was deemed too difficult to understand or forecast, he stayed away.

"Investors should remember that their scorecard is not computed using Olympic-diving methods: Degree-of-difficulty doesn't count," Buffett wrote in his 1994 letter to Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%) (BRKB +0.37%) shareholders. "If you are right about a business whose value is largely dependent on a single key factor that is both easy to understand and enduring, the payoff is the same as if you had correctly analyzed an investment alternative characterized by many constantly shifting and complex variables."

At this point, Nvidia's business is more like the latter than the former. Huang's actions and the potential repercussions leave many unanswered questions for investors. The high level of uncertainty about Nvidia's future explains why it trades at such a low multiple. It's not fear; it's a rational response to the recent events impacting the company.

There are a couple of alternatives to Nvidia stock trading at earnings multiples that aren't much higher than the chip leader.

Buffett himself initiated a position in Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) in 2025. His thesis was based on the company's ability to deploy huge sums of capital with a high return on investment. Specifically, Buffett was talking about its Google Cloud Platform and its data centers full of GPUs and custom silicon.

Alphabet is well-positioned to deliver high returns on invested capital in Google Cloud because of its full-stack approach to AI. It designs the systems and chips in its data centers; it offers a full cloud platform for developers (not just infrastructure); it develops a frontier large language model; and it integrates AI capabilities across its products.

Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said that its payback period for the average server in its data centers is just two years, and its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems break even within half that time. With a useful life of six years and a good operating margin, that's an exceptional return on invested capital. That return on invested capital is set to climb as more spending shifts from data center shells to revenue-generating servers.

Another company positioned to grow based on a single key factor is Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%). Broadcom is the leading custom AI accelerator design partner, the one Alphabet uses for most of its TPUs. Growing demand for custom silicon, which costs less up front than GPUs and offers better price-performance, should result in its AI chip revenue climbing faster than the competition's for years to come. Its lead is protected by its intellectual property and its close relationship with its foundry partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

While Nvidia currently trades around 16 times earnings expectations, Broadcom's stock price isn't much higher at 17 times forward earnings. Alphabet is more expensive at 21 times forward earnings, but it's arguably the least risky of the group, considering its digital advertising business remains a huge cash cow funding its growth.

#3013. Alphabet Could Be the Safest Way to Own Anthropic. Here’s the Math.

Alphabet owns a piece of Anthropic and also gets paid to supply its computing power, which is a nice way to be on both sides of the AI boom.

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:27PM EST

It didn't take long for some of the early enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) stock to wear off. Shares of the artificial intelligence (AI) company opened at $111.50 on their first day of trading on Nov. 19, but fell below their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 on just the fourth day of trading.

I'm not surprised. Tech IPOs have a history of volatility, and it's particularly difficult to put a valuation on a company growing as quickly as Anthropic.

But there's another way to invest in the company that developed Claude. And the more I look at the numbers, the more I like the idea of buying Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) stock instead.

Alphabet has a sizable ownership stake in Anthropic, and it's also well positioned to earn tens of billions of dollars by leasing computing capacity to the AI lab.

At the time of this writing, Anthropic has a market cap of about $1 trillion. That puts the value of Alphabet's 13.7% ownership stake in it at $137 billion. Every time Anthropic gains $100 billion in market cap, Alphabet's investment increases by $13.7 billion, assuming the tech stalwart doesn’t sell any of its shares.

If Anthropic grows into a $2 trillion company, Alphabet's stake would be worth $274 billion. And if Anthropic becomes a $3 trillion company, Alphabet would be sitting on an investment worth $411 billion.

Alphabet only becomes a stronger, wealthier company as Anthropic grows. That's a nice position to be in. And it doesn't even factor in that Anthropic also will be paying a lot to Google Cloud for its services.

Anthropic's S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission revealed that the company is committed to spending at least $121.3 billion for Google Cloud services between April 2026 and July 2033.

That works out to roughly $16.7 billion annually over the life of the agreement, although the actual payments won't necessarily be spread out evenly over those years.

What's particularly attractive about this agreement from Alphabet's perspective is that Anthropic is obligated to pay for the contracted computing capacity regardless of how much it actually uses. If Anthropic's needs fall short of its commitment, it generally still has to pay Google the difference, subject to certain contractual adjustments and exceptions.

And that's only part of the business relationship.

Anthropic also estimates that it will spend another $125 billion to $150 billion for additional computing capacity powered by Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). They are the custom AI chips that Alphabet designs in conjunction with Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%).

Anthropic can obtain that computing capacity directly from Google or through third-party providers. We don't know how much of that money will end up in Alphabet's coffers, and the payments depend on several factors, including how much capacity is made available.

But Alphabet has an opportunity to do considerably more business with Anthropic than the $121.3 billion commitment suggests.

There's an important distinction between investing in Anthropic and doing business with Anthropic.

The AI company generated $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter, but it has also committed to spending approximately $900.9 billion, nearly all of it related to computing and infrastructure.

Anthropic needs to generate enough revenue from Claude to justify those expenditures. Alphabet, meanwhile, is being paid to provide some of that infrastructure.

And most importantly, Alphabet isn't entirely dependent on Anthropic for its success. It has its own AI platform, Gemini, a fast-growing cloud computing business that serves customers beyond Anthropic, and a highly profitable advertising business built around Google Search.

I think Anthropic could be an outstanding company over the next decade, but I'm much less certain about what its stock will do in the next year or two.

That's why I like Alphabet stock here. Anthropic could be a disappointing investment for its shareholders yet remain an extremely valuable customer for Google Cloud. I don't need to get Anthropic's valuation right to make money by owning Alphabet stock.

Grants don’t have to be repaid, but the money can only go toward school-related costs. Here’s how to use grants to pay for school and how to make them go further.

Grants are one of the best ways you can pay for your education. It’s free money you aren’t expected to pay back.

Grants can be used for tuition, course materials and other cost-of-attendance expenses. Some grants, depending on who awards them, require an application or have requirements you must meet before you can get your money.

Here’s how to use a college grant and what it can pay for.

Federal grants come from the federal government.

State grants come from state programs and often can only be used at schools in that state.

Institutional grants come from your college or university, or even your program or major.

Private grants come from nonprofits, community organizations and individual donors.

To receive a federal grant, you must complete the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA). Most states require the FAFSA for state grants, and a few require a separate state application. You’ll need to complete the FAFSA for each year you’re enrolled in school. You may need to meet certain eligibility requirements, such as income limits, to get some grants. The FAFSA is how you apply for the Pell Grant, which is a financial need-based grant. The FAFSA also determines eligibility for federal work-study, which is a job program rather than a grant.

Federal aid, including federal grants, typically requires students to meet satisfactory academic progress. This means you have to maintain a minimum grade point average and be on track to finish your degree on time, as determined by your school. Your school also sets how many credits you must take to qualify for grant funding.

Some grants — typically private or institutional grants — require an additional application that asks for transcripts, letters of recommendation and personal essays. Your school’s financial aid office or the grant provider will have details on applying for specific grants.

After you submit the FAFSA, you’ll receive a financial aid award letter from each school you applied to, which outlines how much in federal, state and institutional grants you’ve been offered. You must accept your aid to receive it.

Most grants will be disbursed directly to your college or university. Your school will apply the grant money first to tuition, fees and any other charges it bills, such as housing or a meal plan.

In some cases, you may receive more grant money than your school bills, which is the best-case scenario. If that happens to you, any leftover funds will likely be refunded to you. Refund timelines vary by school, so it may take some time to get your money. You can get your refund faster by setting up direct deposit with your school. You can then use the funds for other costs approved by your grant — some examples are detailed below.

If you have questions about your grant money, contact your college’s financial aid office.

Grants can help cover cost-of-attendance expenses. Generally, you can use grant money to pay for tuition, textbooks, class materials, transportation, housing and food. Depending on your school’s policies, you can use grant money to cover summer classes or study abroad programs, too.

Some grants come with specific terms about how you can spend them. Check your financial aid award letter or, for a private or institutional grant, the school’s or organization’s website to find specifics.

After your grant is applied to your tuition and school expenses, you can options to fill the gaps between what the grant covers and the total cost of your program. Some options include savings, scholarships, work-study, payment plans, federal student loans or, as a last resort, private loans. By using grants to pay for your college education, you may be able to borrow less.

To maximize the grants you’re eligible to receive, enter accurate information on the FAFSA and complete it as soon as you can — some funds are first-come, first-served. Also, don’t limit yourself to federal or state grants — search and apply for as many privately funded grants as you can find.

Your grant money usually goes straight to your college or university to pay your tuition and fees. Anything that is left over may be disbursed to you for other school-related costs.

Yes, but it depends on your grant. Housing is part of your cost of attendance, so you can use grant money to pay for off-campus rent.

You don’t have to pay back a grant as long as you continue to meet all requirements for the grant, such as staying enrolled. You can use grant money on school and school-related expenses. Some grants may require you to meet eligibility requirements such as a minimum GPA or state residency. If you receive more grant money than your cost of attendance for a given school term, ask your financial aid office if you can put that grant money toward next year’s cost of attendance.

If you have a federal grant like a Pell Grant, these are examples when you may have to repay all or part of the grant:

You received enough scholarship money to reduce your federal aid need.

It depends. You can usually use grant money to buy a laptop. Computers are considered course materials, which fall under cost-of-attendance expenses, so they can be covered by a grant. However, always double-check with the grant provider and your financial aid award letter to ensure that you’re following all restrictions. Whether you can use grant money to cover a laptop depends on your school’s policies and how much grant money you receive.

If you get more grant money than your school bills you, you’ll likely receive the leftover money to spend on other cost-of-attendance expenses. You can use this money on living costs such as transportation or housing. Grant money often goes mostly toward tuition, so a refund isn’t guaranteed.

Grant and scholarship money is generally tax-free when you use it for tuition, required fees, books and required class supplies. If you have additional questions, consider talking to a tax professional.

#3009. Here's What Would Prove Me Wrong About Netflix Stock

The streaming giant's stock looks cheap to me around $60. Three numbers might change my mind.

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:41PM EST

This month, I've argued Netflix (NFLX +0.92%) stock is worth buying near $60, mostly because the streaming giant's profits keep rising even as its sales growth cools. The shares ended Wednesday, Nov. 25, at $59.41. That put them just over their Nov. 20 close of $56.73, the lowest since May 2024, and about 56% under their highest close ever, $133.91 on June 30, 2025 (adjusted for last year's 10-for-1 split).

At $59.41, shares sell for around 16 times earnings, using analysts' average estimate for 2027. In comparison, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) was at 17.1 times forward earnings, according to a Nov. 20 FactSet report.

But what would prove me wrong? Any one of three things would: total view hours (the time members spend watching) down from a year earlier, 2027 ad revenue below $3 billion, or a 2027 operating margin target under 32%. Each would suggest a weaker business than the price assumes.

Much of the streaming service's growth comes from hiking prices, which usually works only while members keep watching. They still are. In the first half of 2026, members watched more than 97 billion hours on Netflix, up 2% year over year and a bit faster than the 1.5% gain in all of 2025.

Members also took this year's price hikes much as they took past ones, management said in October.

But 2% is slow growth, and management knows it. In its third-quarter shareholder letter, Netflix acknowledged "some investor concern about our view hours growth" and said it wants to speed up that growth.

The next test is in the first quarter of 2027, when Netflix plans to change its viewing report from every six months to once a year. If that report shows total view hours lower than a year before, I'd read it as a sign that members are watching less while paying more. That might make future price hikes tougher to push through.

Advertising was supposed to become Netflix's other big growth engine, and it's taking longer than planned. Ad revenue climbed more than 150% in 2025, to over $1.5 billion, and in January, management expected it to roughly double this year. In October, Netflix said it now expects around $2.7 billion instead, because some of its ad features have rolled out a bit more slowly than planned.

Even $2.7 billion would be fast growth, just slower than 2025's rate and the original plan. And Netflix plans to launch its ad-supported tier in 15 more countries in 2027, starting with 12 of them in March.

My bar is the $3 billion Netflix first expected for this year. If 2027 ad revenue can't top that level, even with another year plus 15 new countries, I'd see the issue as more than a slow rollout.

My case leans hardest on Netflix's operating margin. Management expects it to reach 31.5% in 2026, up from 26.7% in 2024, and says that implies operating income growth of over 20% this year. This widening margin is a big reason earnings per share can keep climbing faster than sales.

"[O]ur intent is to grow our operating margin each year," the company wrote in its January shareholder letter, adding that the size of each year's rise will vary.

Even my more cautious forecasts assume the margin improves by half a point a year. That makes Netflix's 2027 margin target, which management says it'll share in January, the figure I'll watch most closely. A target under 32% might mean Netflix must spend more just to keep growing. And it would leave my earnings forecasts for the next few years too high.

Debt isn't on my list. Netflix finished September with net debt (debt minus cash) of around $7.1 billion, under half the operating income it expects this year.

None of the three has happened. View hours are still climbing, ad revenue should still jump this year, and Netflix still expects its operating margin to hit 31.5%.

For now, my case stands, and at roughly $59 I think the growth stock is still worth a look. But if Netflix's fourth-quarter report includes a 2027 margin target below 32% or an ad revenue forecast under $3 billion, I'd need to rethink that.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

TL;DR: Rising inflation could, counterintuitively, help push mortgage rates further down.

Mortgage rates are a little lower this morning, and where they'll go next isn't totally clear.

The average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed-rate mortgage ticked down to 7.05% APR, according to rates provided to NerdWallet by Zillow. This is eight basis points lower than yesterday and 33 basis points lower than a week ago. (A basis point is one one-hundredth of a percentage point.)

Inflation data out this morning looks, at first glance, like bad news for mortgage rates. But depending on how markets react, we could actually see lower mortgage rates. Keep reading after the charts for all the details.

Below are the average APRs we're seeing today, as well as movement over the past month for perspective.

P.S. Markets will be closed tomorrow for Thanksgiving, and Black Friday's a half day, and mortgage rates don't move much when the markets aren't moving. I won't be here to talk to you about mortgage rates, either, 'cause NerdWallet gives us Thursday and Friday off. Happy Thanksgiving!

» Take the next step: Compare mortgage rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

Mortgage rates are constantly changing, since a major part of how rates are set depends on reactions to new inflation reports, job numbers, Fed meetings, global news ... you name it. For example, even tiny changes in the bond market can shift mortgage pricing.

Like I mentioned above, it's not totally obvious where mortgage rates will head next. Let's walk through the two scenarios.

Here's why rates could go up: This morning, we got October's Personal Consumption Expenditures price index, also known as PCE. It's the last measure of inflation to come out each month, but it's also the Federal Reserve's preferred metric, so PCE gets a lot of attention.

The stats came in mostly as predicted, though it's not like the predictions were good — inflation's been overly strong for a while. But the core year-over-year figure, which came in a tenth of a percent over predictions, could prove troublesome. Core PCE removes categories that can be extra volatile, so it's considered a measure that shows the underlying trend. In this case, the underlying trend is Not Good.

It's already pretty much a lock that we'll see a rate hike at the Federal Reserve's December meeting, because yes, raising the federal funds rate is the Fed's main tool for taming inflation. The Fed doesn't set mortgage rates, but a rate-hiking cycle from the central bankers definitely keeps upward pressure on borrowing costs.

On the other hand, here's why that same inflation data could help rates go down: Over the past several days, we've watched the stock market go on a wild ride, with the Anthropic IPO and the return of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Yesterday, things weren't looking good for tech stocks, and these inflation numbers could make it even worse.

The amount that tech companies have borrowed to fund AI buildout is a significant concern for investors, since companies will have to cover those costs before investors see any profits. It's already a big task, and if everything costs more thanks to inflation, it's that much harder.

This AI-related anxiety is rough on the stock market, but it's been a boon for Treasury bonds. More demand for bonds pushes up bond prices, which brings down bond yields (basically, the return investors get on a bond). Mortgage rates for 30-year loans are generally benchmarked to the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, so here's why you care about all of this: Lower Treasury yields means lower mortgage rates, too. If investors keep stressing about inflation eating into tech profits, we could see mortgage rates continue to move lower.

That was a lot of info on inflation, but inflation's not the only major metric influencing rates.

Let's back up for a second. The Federal Reserve tries to keep the economy steady by focusing on two key goals, often referred to as the Fed's dual mandate. One side is price stability — keeping inflation reasonable. The other is maximum employment, meaning those who want to work are able to find jobs.

Next week we'll shift our focus to the employment side of the Federal Reserve's mandate, because the first week of the month is always all about employment data. On Tuesday, Dec. 1, we'll kick things off with the Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (JOLTS). JOLTS can tip us off to trends in the labor market; stuff like whether folks are leaving jobs voluntarily or if companies have openings that are going unfilled.

On Wednesday, payroll firm ADP will release its monthly employment stats. ADP is looking at its own payroll data to get an idea of how the job market is growing or contracting. The numbers don't include the public sector, but ADP often provides a preview of how the jobs report will go.

The Employment Situation Summary, better known as the jobs report, drops on Friday. This is the big one, since it tells us the nation's unemployment rate. The jobs report's other major stat is, similar to ADP, how many jobs the economy added or lost in the previous month. Unlike ADP though, the jobs report is inclusive of everybody in the public and private sectors.

Lately the labor market's been looking super healthy, which is great news for the economy but less positive for mortgage rates. When hiring's strong, the Fed can feel safer raising the federal funds rate (that's the short-term borrowing rate the central bankers adjust). Higher rates tend to discourage businesses from borrowing and expanding, so if the job market's on shaky footing, the central bankers are going to be cautious about raising the benchmark rate.

What we're seeing now though, where inflation is clearly the problem and employment's just fine, is a recipe for higher rates. Again, the Fed doesn't control mortgage rates, but the central bank being in rate-hike mode puts upward pressure on mortgage rates.

If we were to see employment falter in this latest round of numbers, it still probably wouldn't change the Fed's plan. That would be one poor month for the labor market versus months upon months of inflation running rampant — so yeah, they'll keep an eye on jobs, but inflation's still the scourge.

Our most likely source of lower mortgage rates in the short term is what I described above; investors who are leery of inflation and the promise of AI looking to the safe harbor of the bond market.

» Learn more: How the Fed affects mortgage rates

Refinancing might make sense if today’s rates are at least 0.5 to 0.75 of a percentage point lower than your current rate (and if you plan to stay in your home long enough to break even on closing costs).

With rates where they are right now, you could start considering a refi if your current rate is around 7.55% or higher — but there just aren't too many people for whom that's true.

Also consider your goals: Are you trying to lower your monthly payment, shorten your loan term or turn home equity into cash? For example, you might be more comfortable with paying a higher rate for a cash-out refinance than you would for a rate-and-term refinance, so long as the overall costs are lower than if you kept your original mortgage and added a HELOC or home equity loan.

If you're looking for a lower rate, use NerdWallet's refinance calculator to estimate savings and understand how long it would take to break even on the costs of refinancing.

» Time to refi? Compare refinance rates from NerdWallet’s top lenders

There is no universal “right” time to start shopping — what matters is whether you can comfortably afford a mortgage now at today’s rates.

If the answer is yes, don’t get too hung up on whether you could be missing out on lower rates later; you can refinance down the road. Focus on getting preapproved, comparing lender offers, and understanding what monthly payment works for your budget.

NerdWallet’s affordability calculator can help you estimate your potential monthly payment. If a new home isn’t in the cards right now, there are still things you can do to strengthen your buyer profile. Take this time to pay down existing debts and build your down payment savings. Not only will this free up more cash flow for a future mortgage payment, it can also get you a better interest rate when you’re ready to buy.

If you already have a quote you’re happy with, you should consider locking your mortgage rate, especially if your lender offers a float-down option. A float-down lets you take advantage of a better rate if the market drops during your lock period.

Rate locks protect you from increases while your loan is processed, and with the market forever bouncing around, that peace of mind can be worth it.

In addition to market factors outside of your control, your customized quote depends on your:

Even two people with similar credit scores might get different rates, depending on their overall financial profiles.

#3007. Robinhood shares fall as crypto slump weighs on profits, offsetting gains in new businesses

Robinhood shares were down around 8% in pre-market trading on Wednesday as investors digested weaker-than-expected third-quarter earnings despite growth in options trading and prediction markets.

Here's how the brokerage performed in its quarter ended Sept. 30, compared with Wall Street estimates, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:

Robinhood's net income fell to $468 million, or 51 cents per share, from $556 million, or 61 cents per share, a year ago. Revenue represented a 12% increase from $1.27 billion in the same quarter last year.

Despite that gain, transaction-based revenue of $867 million came in below Wall Street estimates from StreetAccount of $879 million, putting focus on whether Robinhood can sustain momentum across its trading businesses and reduce its reliance on volatile market activity.

Robinhood has been diversifying its business as it tries to expand its brokerage app into a broader financial services platform. Options trading and event contracts have become increasingly important sources of transaction revenue, while the company has continued to invest in wealth management, subscriptions and other offerings.

Transaction-based revenue grew 19% from the same period last year to $867 million, driven primarily by a more than 500% increase in event contracts revenue. Additionally, options revenue grew 31% to $399 million and equities revenue rose 41% to $121 million.

Those gains were partially offset by cryptocurrency revenue, which fell 55% to $120 million.

Chief Financial Officer Shiv Verma told CNBC event contracts on crypto movements did well in the quarter, offering investors another way to express a view on crypto despite the slump in prices and spot trading.

Net deposits on the Robinhood platform totaled $15.7 billion for the quarter, equal to a 17% annualized growth rate based on total platform assets at the end of Q2 2026. Over the past year, net deposits totaled $71 billion, representing 21% growth compared with total platform assets at the end of Q3 2025.

—With reporting from CNBC's Robert Hum and Kate Rooney

#3005. Nvidia Stock Has Found Its Next Big Catalyst, Making the Stock a Once-in-a-Decade Buying Opportunity.

Nvidia's physical AI revenue is growing at an incredible pace.

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:57PM EST

Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) has been hammered on the market lately. Even a strong set of quarterly results from the company earlier this month couldn't change investor sentiment, before the reinstatement of co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO sparked a massive rally earlier this week.

However, investors will do well to look past the noise and focus on the company's financial performance. Nvidia easily beat Wall Street's expectations for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended Oct. 25). The company's guidance clearly indicates that its incredible growth is sustainable, driven by the data center business that played a central role in boosting its revenue and earnings last quarter.

However, there is another segment that's starting to move the needle for the company, and I won't be surprised to see this business becoming massive over the next decade.

Data centers have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution so far. However, the technology is now moving from data centers into the real world. Physical AI -- the integration of AI into machines and physical objects such as cars, drones, robots, factory equipment, medical equipment, and other devices -- is emerging as the next big growth driver for Nvidia.

Nvidia notes that its physical AI revenue almost tripled year over year in the previous quarter. What's more, Nvidia expects to generate $25 billion in physical AI revenue in fiscal 2027. That's a huge leap over fiscal 2026, when physical AI added $6 billion to Nvidia's top line. The company is on track to clock almost $424 billion in revenue for fiscal 2027, meaning physical AI will account for nearly 6% of its top line this year.

Nvidia's incredible growth in physical AI isn't surprising, as it has been pushing the envelope in this space. Companies such as Caterpillar, Boston Dynamics, LG Electronics, and other robotics companies are using Nvidia's robotics solutions to develop AI-enabled robots. The semiconductor giant also offers a platform to help customers develop and deploy humanoid robots in healthcare, manufacturing, and retail.

It won't be surprising to see Nvidia's physical AI business become significantly bigger over the coming decade. Counterpoint Research estimates that cumulative physical AI shipments could reach 145 million units by 2035. Barclays estimates that the physical AI market could be worth $1.4 trillion in 2035, which means that Nvidia is scratching the surface of a massive growth opportunity.

As such, there is a solid chance that Nvidia's physical AI revenue will grow at a solid clip over the next 10 years, complementing the growth of the company's data center business.

Nvidia stock is down 26% over the past month. As a result, investors can now buy it at just 16.7 times earnings. The forward earnings multiple of 9.3 is even more attractive for a company whose earnings are poised to double this year. Additionally, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth estimate by five percentage points to 75%.

Analysts have raised their earnings per share (EPS) expectations for the next couple of years, which isn't surprising considering that the company is already sitting on a lucrative multi-year growth opportunity in AI data center infrastructure.

NVDA EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Nvidia noted on the latest earnings call that the cloud industry's backlog now sits at a whopping $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago. This huge backlog will ensure that hyperscalers and AI companies continue to invest in more chips, and that's great news for Nvidia considering that it controls 75% of the AI chip market.

The emergence of additional catalysts, such as physical AI, could help Nvidia consistently beat Wall Street's expectations, improving investor confidence in the stock. So, even though Nvidia has taken a beating lately, its growth prospects are still solid. That's why opportunistic investors may consider capitalizing on this AI stock’s recent slide before it becomes a long-term winner.

#2999. Ready for ‘The Great Lock In’? Viral Money Trend Can Improve Focus

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. With the exception of mortgage, home equity and other home-lending products or services, partner compensation is one of several factors that may affect which products we highlight and where they appear on our site. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

Winter is the ideal time to make progress on your financial goals.

When it’s cold outside, it’s the ideal time to stay home, organize your finances, set some new money goals and make progress toward them.

That’s the promise of the viral winter money trend known as “The Great Lock In” that’s circulating on social media.

“You’re probably not doing too much,” says Robert Baird, wealth manager at Cornerstone Financial Services in Southfield, Michigan. “It gets dark early. So those can be great months to lock into saving and not spend in excess.”

One important component of the Great Lock In is developing new routines that will last well into 2027, says Jordan Mangaliman, founder and fiduciary wealth advisor at GoldLine Wealth Management in Fullerton, California.

“We want a long-term habit versus a Band-Aid fix,” he says. “In today’s economy, money goes in and out so blindingly fast.”

Ready to join the movement? Here’s how to get started.

What’s your money moonshot? Maybe it’s paying off all your credit card debt or purchasing a home. Or spending less than you earn. Defining it is the first step toward achieving it.

“Spend a lot of time identifying what that goal is,” Baird says. “Everyone’s in a different position, so comparing yourself to what you see online might not be applicable.”

Even while setting ambitious money goals, it’s worth grounding them in reality, Mangaliman says.

If you want to save a larger portion of your income, he suggests trying the new saving pattern for a couple of months to see how it feels rather than saying you’ll do it forever and then getting frustrated.

“It’s a marathon, not a sprint,” Mangaliman adds.

Once you’ve outlined those big goals for your Great Lock In, create a budget to help you achieve them, Baird says.

He suggests combing through your previous credit or debit card spending to see where your money is going. Then you can decide what you want to change or shift. Using a tool like the 50/30/20 budget calculator can also help. This approach allots 50% of take-home pay toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward savings and debt payments beyond the minimum.

Baird suggests including saving as a line item in your budget so you don’t forget to do it. “Building that cost into your budget will put you in a better position later,” he says.

Any Great Lock In should include growing your savings, because that makes achieving other goals easier, Baird says.

“Maybe there’s something you could cut in the short term to build up that savings,” he says. Good targets include subscription services, food delivery, entertainment and travel costs.

Saving more is especially challenging in today’s environment, when everyday expenses like gas are higher than they were a year ago.

Baird says that makes winter a good time to try to reduce costs. There can be fewer temptations to go out and spend money when the days are shorter and the temperatures are colder.

Mangaliman recommends setting aside three to six months’ worth of expenses, although even a smaller amount is helpful. “Ultimately it’s about what you can afford,” he says. “It’s the foundation of your financial house.”

Along with building savings, paying down high-interest debt is another pillar of the Great Lock In.

With credit card interest rates higher than they were a few years ago, carrying credit card debt has gotten more expensive. “I would consider applying some savings to paying down debt, especially right now when your debt is costing you more than you can earn in savings,” Baird says. (You still want to reserve an emergency fund to cover unexpected expenses.)

“High-interest debt is one of the biggest thieves of wealth,” Mangaliman says. And one way to avoid turning to debt again in the future is to build up that emergency fund so it’s there for you if you need it.

Even when you are committed to a Great Lock In, some hiccups along the way are inevitable. Success depends on continuing anyway.

“It’s like a diet,” Baird says. “Just because you ate ice cream on a Sunday doesn’t mean on Monday you can’t go right back to being disciplined again.”

“Be kind to yourself and do everything in moderation,” Mangaliman suggests. Just wanting to improve your finances is already a great first step, he says.

In fact, he embraces the Great Lock In mentality himself. “There’s an old saying: It’s not how you start, but how you finish,” he says. “And you want to finish the year on a strong note so you carry those habits into 2027 and beyond.”

10 stocks we like better than DigitalOcean ›

Cloud infrastructure stocks have been hammered lately as investors have been rotating out of this sector for multiple reasons.

Inflationary conditions led the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in September, and it could make a similar move in December. A high-interest rate scenario doesn't bode well for companies investing heavily in artificial intelligence (AI) data center infrastructure, as they will have to contend with higher borrowing costs.

This explains why investors have been booking profits in AI infrastructure stocks. DigitalOcean (DOCN -3.09%) has also borne the brunt of the broader sell-off in cloud stocks, with shares of the company losing 55% of their value over the past six months. However, a closer look at DigitalOcean's growth and prospects indicates that the sell-off may be overdone.

DigitalOcean offers on-demand cloud infrastructure services to small and medium-sized companies, developers, and start-ups. DigitalOcean's customers can rent computing resources to run AI workloads in the cloud without investing in expensive infrastructure of their own. The company also offers platform-as-a-service (PaaS) solutions, enabling users to build, customize, and deploy AI applications.

So, DigitalOcean provides a full-stack cloud infrastructure platform that integrates hardware and software. Customers can build AI agents, run business analytics, detect fraud, create chatbots, summarize documents, and perform other tasks using its AI-native cloud platform. The good part is that DigitalOcean's AI services are in solid demand.

The company released its third-quarter results earlier this month, and it became clear that AI is a key catalyst. Its Q3 revenue increased by 40% year over year to $321 million. The company's annual run rate revenue (ARR) also increased by a similar magnitude to $1.28 billion. However, what's worth noting is that DigitalOcean's ARR from AI customers increased by 288% year over year to $376 million.

The robust adoption of DigitalOcean's AI services explains why it expects its revenue growth rate to ramp up next year. DigitalOcean expects its revenue growth to accelerate to 45% year over year in the current quarter. Even better, it sees a 60% jump in revenue next year, which is well above its prior guidance of 50% growth.

Another important point worth noting is that DigitalOcean's software stack is boosting its ARR. I already pointed out that DigitalOcean doesn't make money by just renting out hardware. The company points out that customers are using its software solutions to build and deploy agentic AI applications, which is driving up DigitalOcean's revenue per megawatt (MW) of cloud computing capacity it deploys.

DigitalOcean is on track to end 2026 with 75 MW of active data center capacity. That number is poised to double next year, and it aims to further increase its capacity in 2028. This explains why analysts expect DigitalOcean to clock solid revenue growth in 2028 as well.

DOCN Revenue Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

Importantly, the increasing adoption of its software offerings is poised to drive significant acceleration in earnings per share (EPS) growth.

DOCN EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts

The impressive revenue and earnings growth that DigitalOcean is poised to deliver is likely to send its shares soaring, according to Wall Street.

DigitalOcean's median 12-month price target of $160 implies potential upside of 123%, according to estimates compiled by CNN. It is worth noting that 16 of the 18 analysts covering DigitalOcean rate the stock as a buy.

It is easy to see why analysts are bullish about its stock price trajectory over the coming year. DigitalOcean's growth rate is picking up, and it trades at an attractive 8 times sales right now. The U.S. technology sector has an average sales multiple of 5.6, and the slight premium that DigitalOcean enjoys is attributable to its improving growth profile.

I won't be surprised to see DigitalOcean trading at a slightly higher sales multiple after a year, driven by a stronger top-line jump. Assuming it trades at 10 times sales, and its top line reaches $1.96 billion in 2027, the company's market cap could increase to $19.6 billion. That's 130% higher than the current market cap, suggesting that DigitalOcean indeed has the potential to live up to Wall Street's expectations and skyrocket next year.

#2996. Better Defense Stock to Own in 2027: Lockheed Martin vs. L3Harris Technologies

Lockheed Martin and L3Harris Technologies are defense contractors with huge backlogs.

By James Halley – Nov 26, 2026 at 1:32PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Lockheed Martin ›

Lockheed Martin (LMT +2.15%) and L3Harris Technologies (LHX +1.48%) are top defense stocks. Each stock has its advantages. Lockheed is a more stable stock with lower price volatility and a higher-yielding dividend. L3Harris, on the other hand, is showing more growth and benefits from higher margins.

Lockheed Martin's shares have soared this year, up more than 18% as I write this, while L3Harris' have slumped by more than 13%.

Here's a quick comparison of these two defense stocks.

F-35 Stealth fighter jet. Image source: Lockheed Martin.

Lockheed Martin is a much larger company, with nearly three times L3Harris' market cap and employee count. The company's third-quarter backlog of $292 billion provides around 3.6 years of revenue visibility, substantially deeper than L3Harris' 2.25 years for its $53.2 billion backlog.

Lockheed management is predicting high single-digit growth across all four of its business segments in 2027, led by F-35 sustainment/production and a $52.5 billion multiyear award for PAC-3 MSE interceptor missiles. That scale allows the company to thrive even if one segment falters.

As a specialist in defense electronics, resilient communications, and propulsion, L3Harris generated a 15.9% segment operating margin in the third quarter, roughly 500 basis points higher than Lockheed Martin. L3Harris reported third-quarter earnings per share (EPS) of $3.28, up 33% year over year, prompting management to raise full-year EPS guidance to a range of $12.25 to $12.35, an increase of 44% at the midpoint.

Lockheed, on the other hand, saw its third-quarter EPS slip by 11% to $6.44. It reaffirmed full-year EPS of between $29.35 and $30.25, a 38% gain at the midpoint.

Both companies have above-average dividend yields. At their current share prices, Lockheed's dividend yield is 2.42% while L3Harris' is 1.94%. Lockheed has increased its dividend for 24 consecutive years, while L3Harris has raised its dividend for 25 consecutive years. L3Harris has been more aggressive in increasing its dividend over the past decade, raising it by more than 135%, compared to just more than 89% for Lockheed, which could be an advantage in a stock-to-stock matchup.

Despite its share gain this year, Lockheed's stock is trading at a better price point. Its forward price-to-earnings ratio is slightly more than 18 times earnings estimates compared to more than 20 for L3Harris.

Lockheed's biggest problem is that it is the lead on massive hardware programs, such as the F-35, F-16, C-13, and Sikorsky helicopters, and, as such, has lower operating margins, around 10.8% as of the third quarter. It is also affected more by fixed-price development or production charges. It stands to lose more, too, if a Democratic-controlled Congress tightens defense spending.

L3Harris carries more debt, with a debt-to-earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) ratio of 3.1, compared to 1.9 for Lockheed, and its debt payments could easily weigh on its earnings growth. L3Harris carries a heavier debt load relative to its size, with $9 billion in net long-term debt. Much of that is due to the company's $4.7 billion acquisition of Aerojet Rocketdyne in 2023.

However, L3Harris plans to sell a majority stake in its space propulsion and power Systems business to AE Industrial for $845 million, while retaining a 40% ownership stake in the newly created Rocketdyne venture, which includes manufacturing and selling RS-25 rocket engines.

Deciding which stock is best really comes down to your investing needs. Lockheed certainly offers more stability, though with less growth potential.

L3Harris is expected to see more revenue and earnings growth, though its higher valuation shows some of that expected growth is already priced into the stock. If I had to choose, Lockheed is the safer pick because of its scale, better dividend, and lower valuation.

#2990. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

10 stocks we like better than Caterpillar ›

Looking at Caterpillar's (CAT +0.57%) stock chart lately feels like a market paradox.

On the other hand, the stock has been cut roughly in half from its 52-week high, leaving shares trading at a modest 16.5 times forward earnings.

Even the mining division is seeing healthy order rates for copper and gold operations.

However, management expects 58% of the current backlog to convert into revenue within the next 12 months.

Rather than a temporary double-ordering boost, Caterpillar is backing the demand with physical capacity expansions. The company plans to nearly triple large reciprocating engine production by 2030 along with a $1 billion manufacturing investment in North Carolina.

For long-term investors, the massive backlog provides multi-year revenue visibility as the capacity constraints gradually ease.

#2977. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

We believe everyone should be able to make financial decisions with confidence. While we don't cover every company or financial product on the market, we work hard to share a wide range of offers and objective editorial perspectives.

So how do we make money? Our partners compensate us for advertisements that appear on our site. This compensation helps us provide tools and services - like free credit score access and monitoring. Other factors include your credit profile, product availability and proprietary website methodologies.

However, these factors do not influence our editors' opinions or ratings, which are based on independent research and analysis. Our partners cannot pay us to guarantee favorable reviews. Here is a list of our partners.

You don’t need a basement bunker, but keeping some cash on hand might help.

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

But what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

Dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:

Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, says Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, said Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good plan, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?)

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson said. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”

If your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge says. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”

Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to update your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the big concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he says. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” said Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”

#2973. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2966. The Buffett Indicator Is Flashing Red. These 2 Dividend Stocks Could Be Safe Havens.

The Buffett indicator is well above its long-term average, so you may want to consider buying stocks of companies that sell things people don't want to live without.

By Reuben Gregg Brewer – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:05PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Johnson & Johnson ›

Johnson & Johnson (JNJ -0.91%) and Procter & Gamble (PG +0.44%) sell products that are bought in both good times and bad. That's notable right now because the so-called Buffett indicator is more than two standard deviations above its historical average, suggesting a high risk of a downturn. If you are a conservative investor, safe-haven stocks in the healthcare and consumer staples sectors should be high on your wish list. Here's why.

Warren Buffett was the former CEO of Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%)(BRKB +0.37%). His long-term investment approach resulted in the company achieving incredible long-term returns for investors. A key piece of the story was his penchant for waiting to buy until stock prices were attractive. That meant holding off during periods of overvaluation. The tool he used to determine the valuation of the broader market was the total value of the stock market divided by gross domestic product (GDP).

It is a rough gauge, at best. But when the Buffett indicator is at an extreme level, as it is today, it's worth taking a step back. You may want to reevaluate your portfolio, perhaps holding more cash. Or, if you want to remain invested, increasing your exposure to more conservative dividend stocks that have a history of holding up during periods of economic and market weakness. That's exactly what you'll find with J&J and P&G.

One of the big reasons to like J&J right now is that it is a Dividend King, with the longest dividend streak of any healthcare company at 64 years. It has successfully navigated multiple recessions and bear markets over that span. While the company has changed over the years, it currently focuses on the pharmaceutical and medical device segments of the broader healthcare sector.

The big story is that drugs and medical devices usually aren't optional purchases. Consumers are willing to pay for them because they improve their lives and can sometimes mean the difference between life and death. That makes J&J very resilient, a fact bolstered by its diversification across two business lines.

The one problem is valuation. J&J isn't cheap right now, but for conservative investors, it may be worth paying a premium if the lofty level of the Buffett indicator has you worried. That said, the healthcare giant's 1.9% dividend yield is well above the 1% you'd collect from the S&P 500 index (^GSPC -0.25%) and the healthcare average of roughly 1.3%.

P&G is one of the world's largest consumer staples companies. It has a strong brand portfolio focused on paper products, toiletries, and makeup. Most of its products sit at the high end of their categories, which would seem like a risky place to be during an economic downturn. However, P&G has long focused on innovation, producing products that consumers are willing to pay more for. Notably, despite belt-tightening in many households today, P&G's organic sales grew 4% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027.

And consumers aren't likely to stop buying their favorite toilet paper and toothpaste even if there is a downturn. At least that's what history has shown, helping P&G to increase its dividend for 70 consecutive years. Like J&J, that's the best streak in its peer group.

P&G isn't exactly cheap, either. However, its price-to-sales and price-to-earnings ratios are roughly in line with their five-year averages. That suggests the stock is fairly valued right now. And the stock's 2.5% yield is above the consumer staples average of 2%, so you are getting a generous yield.

The Buffett indicator is flashing bright red warning signs right now, given its elevated level. If that has you thinking about dialing back on risk, you should consider reliable dividend stocks from defensive sectors like healthcare and consumer staples. The best dividend records in those two sectors belong to Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble. It's probably a good idea to start your search with these two safe-haven stocks.

#2964. I'd Buy Anthropic Stock Early — but Only If I Liked the Answers to These 3 Questions

The AI lab's revenue is soaring, but the outlook for its profitability and valuation will determine whether the stock is worth buying at current prices.

By Manali Pradhan, CFA – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:17PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic (ANT +1.08%), the company behind the Claude AI ecosystem, priced its initial public offering (IPO) at $83 per share. However, when trading began on Nov. 19, the stock opened at $111.50, a 34.3% premium to that price. Shares closed at $81.90 on Nov. 24, leaving investors who bought at the opening price with a loss of over 26%.

Still, investor interest in the stock is high. Nearly seven in 10 stock investors surveyed by The Motley Fool said they planned to buy OpenAI, Anthropic, or both at their IPOs.

However, there are three specific questions that investors will want to answer before buying Anthropic stock.

Anthropic's revenue surged more than tenfold from $1.38 billion in the third quarter of 2025 to $16.96 billion in the third quarter of 2026. The number of customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue for Anthropic also increased from more than 950 to over 11,900 in the same time frame. The company had more than 1,900 customers that spent at least $1 million with it on an annualized basis at the end of the third quarter. This indicates that businesses are increasingly spending substantial amounts on the Claude AI ecosystem.

However, Anthropic's revenue depends heavily on customer usage. Consumption-based fees accounted for approximately 79% of revenue in the first nine months of 2026. When businesses expand their use of Claude Code and other applications, they generate more revenue for Anthropic. However, customers could also reduce spending by limiting their token use or by switching to lower-priced AI models or competing services.

Anthropic reported net revenue retention of approximately 900% at the end of September. This highlights the rapid spending growth among the company's existing customers. However, that calculation includes customers who generated as little as $1 in revenue in the prior-year quarter. Hence, the 900% figure may partly reflect rapid expansion from a low starting base rather than a growth rate Anthropic can sustain.

Pricing is another concern. Anthropic disclosed that price reductions and contractual discounts that it introduced in the second and third quarters cut its revenue by approximately $600 million.

With OpenAI's ChatGPT, Alphabet's (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) Gemini, and other artificial intelligence (AI) competitors competing for enterprise customers, Anthropic will need to maintain strong usage growth without sacrificing too much on pricing.

Anthropic reported an operating loss of $567 million in the third quarter, compared with a $974 million profit in the second quarter. However, adjusted operating income increased from $2.24 billion to $2.46 billion. The adjusted figure excludes stock-based compensation and certain other expenses paid in shares rather than cash. Such payments do reduce other shareholders' ownership stakes in the company.

Computing expenses were a major concern. Anthropic's revenue increased sequentially by $5.4 billion in the third quarter, while computing and infrastructure expenses rose by $4.3 billion. Hence, the increase in computing costs was equivalent to nearly 80% of the additional revenue.

Adjusted operating income, however, increased by only $228 million during the same period. Hence, investors need to consider just what fraction of Anthropic's future revenue growth will drop down to the bottom line as profits.

Anthropic's adjusted operating margin declined from 19% in the second quarter to 15% in the third quarter, mainly due to $5 billion in costs associated with leasing computing capacity under expensive short-term deals. The company expects to replace some of that with capacity from cheaper long-term arrangements. However, its continued payments for computing infrastructure could put pressure on cash flow.

Anthropic has firm commitments to spend approximately $900.9 billion on leasing computing and infrastructure, $451.6 billion of which is expected to be spent by the end of 2030. These commitments extend over several years, with some subject to conditions or termination rights.

Anthropic generated $6.57 billion in operating cash flow during the first nine months of 2026. However, it also spent $2.88 billion on equipment purchases and prepayments for leased assets and equipment. Hence, investors should watch whether Anthropic can generate enough cash from operations to fund its growing infrastructure needs.

Anthropic had a market capitalization of approximately $1.1 trillion as of the close of trading on Nov. 24. Hence, the stock was trading at about 31 times its trailing-12-month revenue of $35.28 billion. The valuation multiple drops to around 13.4 times when using Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate of $81 billion at the end of October. However, the run rate reflects recent customer spending rather than revenues earned over a full year.

Both metrics show investors are already paying a substantial premium for Anthropic's expected future growth.

Another concern for investors who buy now is the looming increase in Anthropic’s float — the volume of its shares available for trading. Stakeholders who owned Anthropic shares prior to the IPO are subject to restrictions on selling their shares. But those lock-up periods will expire in a series of tranches from December 2026 through 2027. Each expiration date will allow those early investors to sell a larger fraction of the shares they own. This certainly does not mean these shareholders will sell quickly, but the additional availability of shares to be purchased could put downward pressure on the stock price. Future secondary share issuances could also reduce existing shareholders' ownership stakes in Anthropic.

With all that in mind, I would suggest that you buy Anthropic only if you calculate that its valuation offers sufficient upside potential, despite moderating revenue growth and potential stock dilution.

#2958. Anthropic Stock Is Now Trading as ANT. Should You Buy Today or Wait?

Tech stock IPOs have a long history of disappointing early investors.

By Matthew Benjamin – Nov 26, 2026 at 2:30PM EST

10 stocks we like better than Anthropic ›

Anthropic (ANT +1.08%), the company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude, began trading last week under the ticker symbol ANT following the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history.

After a strong first day, when investors bid the new stock up from its IPO price of $83 to about $111 per share, it has been falling since. Three trading days after its debut, the stock has dropped below its IPO price and traded at around $78 per share.

So, does that make this exciting new stock a buy, given that it's cheaper now?

I would say no. Even investors determined to add this stock to their portfolio should wait. That's because the initial pop in the share price, followed by a downward trend, is nothing new. In fact, IPO stocks have a long history of disappointing early investors.

IPO stocks are exciting, and that excitement often gives their shares an initial market boost. The share price of an IPO stock typically sees a first-day return of 18%, according to research by Edward Jones. Technology stocks do even better on day one, with a 35.2% increase.

But IPO tech stocks then fall, on average, 3% after three months and 14% after six months, according to that same research. So waiting six months, until the stock finds its footing beyond the initial IPO excitement, is your best bet.

#2946. If a Market Correction Is Around the Corner, I'm Making This 1 Easy Move

Don't be scared of corrections. Take advantage of them.

By David Dierking – Nov 26, 2026 at 3:00PM EST

10 stocks we like better than S&P 500 Index ›

Anyone waiting to buy stocks at better prices got a lesson in just how quickly an opportunity can disappear.

Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) CEO Jensen Huang's departure sent some U.S. stock prices sharply lower last week. The S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) entered correction territory, and the Nasdaq-100 briefly sank into a bear market. By Monday morning, Huang was reinstated, and the Nasdaq-100 rebounded by nearly 7%.

How should investors handle this volatility, and what portfolio moves, if any, should you make right now?

This week's rebound was astonishingly quick in that a lot of ground was recovered in a single day. But it does follow a recent track record of rapid recoveries.

The Q1 2025 correction that culminated with President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariffs experienced a similar turnaround. After falling 19% by early April, the S&P 500 was back to all-time highs by the end of June.

Of course, there was the COVID pandemic bear market. The S&P 500 fell by more than 30% in one month's time. After a multitrillion-dollar stimulus package, the index was back to a new all-time high by August, just five months later.

It's rare to find just the right moment to buy the dip as it's happening. That's why I usually suggest keeping your systematic investment plans going as scheduled.

Purchasing shares on a set schedule is an ideal way to make at least some purchases at lower prices without trying to call a market bottom. In sharp, single-day rebounds like Monday, it may not work unless you place a trade manually ahead of time. But during corrections where the recovery process takes months, even a couple of buys along the way can reduce your cost basis significantly.

Keeping your automatic investment plans going throughout the current pullback might be especially important this time around.

A CBOE study last year found that sudden volatility shocks in the markets can result in elevated volatility that lasts for months. Volatility, of course, tends to be closely associated with falling stock prices. If that pattern follows the current correction, it could be a fair amount of time before the S&P 500 and other major equity indexes hit new highs.

But for regular investors, that can be an opportunity. The longer stocks hover below highs, the better your chance to pick up more shares at discounted prices. It may feel counterintuitive as it's happening. But continuing to make systematic monthly investments can pay off significantly in the years ahead.
